parts.answer: Conflict serializable means can be transformed to serial by swapping non-conflicting operations. View serializable means equivalent to serial schedule in terms of reads-from and final writes. Schedule S: R1(X) W2(X) R3(X) W1(Y) R2(Y) W3(Y). This is view serializable to T2,T1,T3 but not conflict serializable because there's a cycle in precedence graph T1->T2, T2->T3, T3->T1. Read-from: T3 reads X from T2, T2 reads Y from T1. Final write: T3 writes Y last.

Thomas' Write Rule ignores obsolete writes based on timestamps. Basic TO aborts conflicting late transactions. Strict 2PL holds locks until commit. In a scenario with T1 older: T1 reads X, T2 writes X. TO aborts T2 if T1 has higher priority. Strict 2PL blocks T2 until T1 commits. Thomas' Write Rule allows T2 write if T1's write is older, ignoring T1's write if it hasn't happened yet.

Canonical query tree has Cartesian product at leaves, then selection, then projection. Apply heuristic: push selection down, replace Cartesian with joins, push projection down. Use rules like breaking selections, combining selections with cross products, moving projections earlier. Optimized tree has selections as close to leaves as possible.

Cost-based optimization uses statistics to estimate execution cost and chooses min cost plan. Heuristic optimization follows rules like push selections. Statistics include histograms, selectivity, cardinality. Correlated subqueries are executed once per outer row which is slow. Decorrelation transforms them to joins. Outdated statistics may cause nested loops instead of hash join because optimizer thinks small table but actually large.

CAP theorem says a distributed system can only have two of Consistency, Availability, Partition Tolerance. Cassandra is AP (eventually consistent). MongoDB is CP by default. Spanner is CP with strong consistency. DynamoDB tunable but usually AP. Tunable consistency allows choosing between strong and eventual based on read/write quorum settings.

For 500M users, use consistent hashing for partitioning by user ID to distribute evenly. Replication factor 3 for availability. Use quorum reads/writes for critical data consistency. For network partition, use hinted handoff and read repair. Conflict resolution with vector clocks: each object has version vector (node, counter). On conflict, return all versions to application or last-write-wins based on timestamps.

Document stores have nested documents. Wide-column stores have column families. Graph databases have nodes and edges. For social network, graph database best because relationships are first-class. Finding friends of friends who liked same post: In Neo4j: MATCH (u:User)-[:FRIEND]->(f)-[:FRIEND]->(fof), (fof)-[:LIKED]->(p:Post) WHERE u.id='123' RETURN fof. In MongoDB need multiple lookups, slower for deep traversals.

B+ Tree: balanced tree structure, all leaves at same level with linked list for range queries. Insertion may cause node splits. Deletion may cause merging. Search O(log n). ISAM: static structure with index levels fixed, good for static data. Linear Hashing: incremental resizing, uses hash function and overflow buckets. Insertion triggers splits when load factor exceeds threshold. B+ Tree best for range queries and dynamic data. ISAM fastest for static read-mostly. Linear hashing best for equality queries on dynamic data.

Bitmap index: arrays of bits for each distinct value, good for low-cardinality columns. R-Tree: spatial index using minimum bounding rectangles, hierarchical. Inverted index: maps words to document IDs. For data warehouse star schema: bitmap indexes on dimension foreign keys in fact table for fast AND/OR operations. B+ Tree on dimensions. Covering indexes include all columns needed by query to avoid table lookup. Materialized views pre-compute aggregations.

Index-only scan reads index without accessing table because all needed columns are in index. GiST is generalized search tree for complex data types. GIN is generalized inverted index for composite values. For JSONB column, GIN with jsonb_path_ops supports path queries. CREATE INDEX idx ON table USING GIN (jsoncol jsonb_path_ops); Queries use @> operator for containment. EXPLAIN ANALYZE shows index scan vs sequential scan. Bitmap index scan builds bitmap of matching rows then fetches.

Conflict serializability: two schedules are conflict equivalent if they have same operations and order of conflicting operations is same. A schedule is conflict serializable if conflict equivalent to some serial schedule. View serializability: less restrictive, considers read-from relationships and final writes. A schedule is view serializable if there exists a serial schedule where all reads see same values and final writes are same. Example: S: W1(X) R2(X) W1(Y) W2(Y) R3(X) W3(Z). Let's construct another: S': R1(X) W2(X) R3(X) W1(Y) R2(Y) W3(Y). Check read-from: T3 reads X written by T2. T2 reads Y written by T1. Final write: T3 writes Y last. Equivalent to T1,T2,T3 serial order. Conflict graph has cycle so not conflict serializable.

Thomas' Write Rule: uses timestamps. If transaction wants to write item and read timestamp is larger, write is ignored. Basic Timestamp Ordering: checks both read and write timestamps. If read timestamp is larger than transaction timestamp, abort. If write timestamp is larger, abort. Strict 2PL: uses locks, holds exclusive locks until commit. For operations on X,Y,Z: Assume T1 older than T2. T1 reads X. T2 writes X (TS=10, read-TS=5 from T1). TO aborts T2. Thomas allows the write? No, if T1 hasn't written X yet, Thomas' Write Rule only ignores writes where the item's write timestamp already larger. Strict 2PL would block T2 until T1 releases X lock. Starvation possible in TO if transaction always restarted. Cascading rollback avoided in Strict 2PL due to exclusive locks until commit.

Given query: SELECT dept_name, AVG(salary) FROM employee e JOIN department d ON e.dept_id = d.id WHERE e.age > 30 GROUP BY d.name HAVING AVG(salary) > 50000. Initial tree: PROJECT(dept_name, AVG(salary)) -> HAVING -> GROUP BY -> SELECT(age>30) -> JOIN(e.dept_id=d.id) -> CROSS(employee, department). Heuristic optimization: push SELECT(age>30) below JOIN. Convert CROSS to JOIN. Push projection to reduce columns early: only keep e.dept_id, e.salary, e.age, d.id, d.name. After applying rules: PROJECT -> HAVING -> GROUP BY -> JOIN -> (SELECT(age>30) on employee projected, department projected). Cost estimation: materialized needs temp storage for intermediate results. Pipelined streams directly, saves I/O.

Cost-based uses statistics (row count, distinct values, histograms) to compute cost of each plan. Uses formulas for I/O and CPU. Heuristic uses transformation rules without cost evaluation. Statistics important: selectivity = 1/distinct values. Histograms show data distribution. Correlation between predicates is an issue. Correlated subqueries: for each outer row, inner executes. Decorrelation: rewrite as JOIN or use semi-join. Example: SELECT * FROM emp e WHERE salary > (SELECT AVG(salary) FROM emp WHERE dept=e.dept). Decorrelated: SELECT e.* FROM emp e JOIN (SELECT dept, AVG(salary) avg_sal FROM emp GROUP BY dept) d ON e.dept=d.dept WHERE e.salary > d.avg_sal. Optimizer error example: skewed data, uniform assumption underestimates result size, picks nested loop instead of hash join, causing poor performance.

CAP Theorem (Brewer): in a distributed data store, you can guarantee only two of Consistency (all nodes see same data), Availability (every request gets response), Partition Tolerance (system works despite network partitions). Since partitions are inevitable, systems must choose between C and A. Cassandra: AP, uses eventual consistency with tunable consistency levels. MongoDB: CP in replica set mode (primary-secondary, if primary fails, no writes until new primary elected). Spanner: CP, uses TrueTime API and atomic clocks for external consistency, strongly consistent. DynamoDB: AP default with eventual consistency, also offers strongly consistent reads at cost. Tunable consistency: in Cassandra, you can set consistency level (ONE, QUORUM, ALL) for both reads and writes. QUORUM ensures majority overlap, giving strong consistency if R+W > replication factor.

Design for 500M user social platform: Sharding/Partitioning: Use consistent hashing by user_id for user data, by post_id for post data. This gives even distribution and minimal data movement when scaling. Replication: 3 copies per shard using multi-leader or leader-follower across regions. Consistency: critical (financial): use Paxos/Raft for leader election and synchronous replication. Non-critical (likes, timeline): eventual consistency with CRDTs. CRDTs: use G-Counter (grow-only counter) for likes; LWW-Register (last-writer-wins) for post content updates; OR-Set (observed-remove set) for follower lists. Vector clocks: each object has [node1:5, node2:3]. On update, increment own counter. Conflict: if concurrent updates, merge by union of sets or max. Network partition handling: nodes continue accepting writes, when healed, use anti-entropy (Merkle trees) to sync differences.

Document store (MongoDB): JSON/BSON documents, flexible schema, embedded documents for 1:1, references for 1:N. Good for product catalogs. Wide-column store (Cassandra): tables with rows and dynamic columns grouped into column families, optimized for writes. Good for time-series, IoT. Graph (Neo4j): native graph storage with nodes, relationships, properties, optimized for traversals. For social network: Graph database is best because data is highly connected. Query 'friends of friends who liked same post': Neo4j Cypher: MATCH (me:User {id:'u1'})-[:FRIEND]->(f1:User)-[:FRIEND]->(f2:User), (f2)-[:LIKED]->(p:Post) WHERE (me)-[:LIKED]->(p) RETURN DISTINCT f2. This is a few pointer traversals, constant time per relationship. MongoDB: db.users.aggregate([{$match:{id:'u1'}}, {$lookup...}, {$unwind}, {$lookup...}]) requires multiple $lookup operations, scanning indexes repeatedly, much slower for deep traversals (2+ hops).

B+ Tree: Balanced multi-level index. Structure: internal nodes have keys and pointers to children, leaf nodes have all keys and data pointers (or values), with sibling pointers forming linked list. Insertion: search leaf, insert, if overflow (order d, max 2d keys), split into two nodes and promote middle key. Can cascade splits upward. Deletion: find key, delete, if underflow (< d keys), borrow from sibling if possible, else merge and adjust parent. Search: O(log_d n) I/Os. ISAM: index sequential access method. Static structure with index levels and data in sequential file. Fast for static data, but insertion overflow handled by overflow chains, degrading to linear search. Linear Hashing: dynamic hashing using family of hash functions h0, h1, h2... Initially h0 covers all buckets. When load factor exceeds threshold, split bucket (add new bucket), rehash with next function. Addresses round-robin. No directory needed. Comparison: B+ Tree best for range queries (linked leaves), rebalancing overhead. ISAM best for read-only data. Linear Hashing good for equality search with growth. Fill factor: lower fill means more empty space but less splits. Higher fill better space utilization but more frequent splits.

Bitmap indexes: each distinct value gets bitmap (array of 1s and 0s). Fast bitwise AND, OR, NOT for low cardinality columns (gender, status). Compact for low cardinality. Not efficient for high cardinality or frequent updates. R-Trees: spatial index for multi-dimensional data. Structure like B-Tree but keys are bounding rectangles. Good for range queries on spatial data (nearby points, containment). Inverted index: used for full-text search. Maps each word (term) to list of document IDs and positions. Star schema indexing strategy: Fact table: bitmap indexes on all foreign keys to dimension tables (date_key, product_key, store_key). These are low cardinality in dimension context but allow fast intersection using bitmaps. Dimension tables: B+ Tree indexes on primary keys and frequently filtered columns. Covering indexes: include non-key columns to avoid table access. Example: CREATE INDEX idx_covering ON fact_sales(sale_date) INCLUDE (amount, quantity); for query SELECT amount, quantity WHERE sale_date = '2025-01-01' avoids key lookup. Materialized views: pre-compute and store aggregations like daily sales sum. Query rewriter uses materialized view instead of scanning fact table. Bitmap join index: creates bitmap from dimension values into fact table rows, answering complex filters efficiently.

Index-only scan (covering index scan): All columns required by query are present in the index key or included columns. The database reads the index without touching the table heap. Faster because fewer I/Os, no heap fetches. Regular index scan: reads index to find row pointers, then fetches rows from table. PostgreSQL GiST (Generalized Search Tree): balanced tree structure, extensible framework. Supports geometric data types, full-text search, arrays. Each internal node contains a predicate that holds for all entries in its subtree. Query traverses nodes where predicate is consistent. GIN (Generalized Inverted Index): inverted index structure. Good for composite values like arrays, JSONB. Contains posting lists mapping key values to row IDs. Two-phase: first looks up keys in B-tree, then scans posting tree/heap. For JSONB: CREATE INDEX idx_json ON table USING GIN (data jsonb_path_ops); jsonb_path_ops optimizes for @> (exists) operator, smaller index. Query: SELECT * FROM table WHERE data @> '{"name":"John"}'. Planner uses GIN index via bitmap index scan. EXPLAIN ANALYZE: 'Bitmap Index Scan on idx_json' then 'Bitmap Heap Scan on table'. Index Scan for B-tree. Sequential Scan scans entire table (cost highest). Bitmap scan: builds bitmap of matching TIDs, sorts by page, reads heap pages once (good for moderate selectivity). Index scan: directly fetches heap rows via TIDs, good for high selectivity (few rows).

Conflict serializability uses precedence graph. If graph has no cycle, schedule is conflict serializable. View serializability is broader, includes schedules not conflict serializable. Example schedule: T1: R(A) W(A), T2: W(A) W(B), T3: R(B) W(B). Blind writes occur. View equivalent to T1,T2,T3. Conflict graph has cycle T2 writes A then T1 reads it, T3 reads B from T2. Also T1->T2 due to A? Actually need to work through step by step. Suppose schedule: R1(A), W2(A), W1(B), R2(B), R3(A), W3(A). Read from: T2 reads B from T1. T3 reads A from T2. Final write of A: T3. Serial schedule T1,T2,T3: R1(A) W1(A) W1(B) R2(A) W2(B) R3(A) W3(A) - reads differ so not equivalent.

Thomas' Write Rule modification of Basic TO. Checks timestamp of data item. If TS(T) < W-timestamp of data item, write ignored (obsolete). If TS(T) < R-timestamp, abort. Basic TO aborts for any conflict with later timestamp. Strict 2PL: transactions must acquire shared lock before read, exclusive lock before write, hold all exclusive locks until commit. Scenario: T1(TS=10), T2(TS=20). T1:R(X), T2:W(X). Basic TO: T2's write-timestamp request: item's read-TS=10 < 20 so allowed? Actually T2 writing, check read-TS: if read-TS > TS(T2) abort. read-TS=10 < 20 OK. Check write-TS: write-TS=0 < 20 OK. So allowed. Wait no, if T2 writes X and then T1 reads later? The scenario order matters. If T1 reads X first (read-TS becomes 10), then T2 writes: write allowed. If T2 writes first (write-TS=20), then T1 reads: T1's TS=10 < write-TS=20, so abort T1. Thomas' Write Rule ignores T1 write attempt if write-TS already > TS(T1). Strict 2PL: T1 gets S-lock on X, reads. T2 requests X-lock on X, waits because T1 holds S-lock. T1 commits, releases locks, T2 gets X-lock. No starvation in Strict 2PL, no cascading rollback because no dirty reads possible (exclusive locks held until EOT).

Query: SELECT c.name, SUM(o.amount) FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON c.id=o.cust_id WHERE c.region='West' AND o.date > '2025-01-01' GROUP BY c.name HAVING SUM(o.amount) > 1000. Initial canonical tree: PROJECT -> HAVING -> GROUP BY -> SELECT(region AND date) -> JOIN(c.id=o.cust_id) -> CROSS(customers, orders). Optimization: split selection: region push to customers, date push to orders. Replace CROSS with JOIN. Push projection: only columns needed (c.id, c.name, c.region, o.cust_id, o.amount, o.date). Optimized: PROJECT -> HAVING -> GROUP BY -> JOIN -> [SELECT(region) PROJ(customers), SELECT(date) PROJ(orders)]. Pipelining: operators produce tuples on the fly, consumer processes without writing to disk. Materialization: intermediate results written to disk. Pipelined evaluation reduces I/O cost, better for memory-resident data. I/O cost calculation: B(customers)=100 blocks, B(orders)=1000 blocks. Nested loop join cost if orders outer: 100+100*1000=100,100 block accesses (materialized nested loop). Index nested loop with index on orders.cust_id: 100+100*1=200. Hash join cost: 3*(100+1000)=3300 with partitioning.

Cost-based optimization: enumerates plans, estimates cost using statistics (relation sizes, distinct values, histograms). Chooses lowest estimated cost plan. Uses dynamic programming or genetic algorithms. Heuristic: applies rules like 'push selections down', 'perform projections early', 'replace cross product with joins'. No cost evaluation, guarantees not worst plan but not necessarily optimal. Statistics: histograms capture distribution (equi-width, equi-depth). Selectivity = (number of tuples satisfying condition) / total. Cardinality = selectivity * total rows. Correlation between predicates often unaccounted. Correlated subquery inefficiency: executed per outer row. Decorrelation: transform EXISTS subquery to semi-join, scalar subquery to outer join with group by. Example: SELECT * FROM emp WHERE dept_id IN (SELECT id FROM dept WHERE budget > 1M). Decorrelated: SELECT emp.* FROM emp JOIN dept ON emp.dept_id = dept.id WHERE dept.budget > 1M. Optimizer suboptimal plan scenario: a column with 99% NULL but optimizer assumes uniform distribution, estimates higher selectivity, chooses index scan but sequential scan would be better. PostgreSQL uses auto-analyze to update stats, but between analyzes, stats can become stale leading to bad plan selection.

CAP theorem: Consistency (linearizability), Availability (all non-failing nodes respond), Partition tolerance (continues operating despite arbitrary message loss). In practice, network partitions happen, so distributed databases must choose CP or AP. Cassandra: AP, uses eventual consistency, consistency level determines how many replicas must respond. Write to QUORUM, read from QUORUM gives strong consistency (R+W > N). MongoDB replica set: CP, primary-secondary replication. If primary fails, election occurs; no writes accepted during election (lose availability). Spanner: CP, uses GPS and atomic clocks (TrueTime) for global consistency across data centers. External consistency (strongest). DynamoDB: AP default (eventually consistent reads), optionally strongly consistent reads (uses more resources). Tunable consistency: client can specify consistency level per operation. For example, write to ALL (all replicas) ensures no stale reads but if any replica down, write fails (sacrificing availability).

Partitioning: hash by user_id for user-related data, hash by post_id for post data. This spreads load evenly. Regional sharding: users in Asia-Pacific mapped to shards in Singapore region, European users to Frankfurt shards, etc., for latency. Replication: each shard replicated within region (leader-follower for writes, multi-region async replication). Consistency: critical operations (payments, ad transactions) use 2PC or Percolator-style two-phase commit across shards. Non-critical (posts, likes): eventual consistency with CRDTs. LWW-Register for post content (timestamp resolution). G-Counter for likes (merge by max). OR-Set for friends list (observed remove, tracks which elements were removed). Using vector clocks: each update includes [node_id, counter]. Merge: take max counters per node. Conflict: if concurrent updates to same field, use application-level merge (e.g., set union for tags). Network partition: regions become independent islands. When healed, use Merkle trees to sync divergent data efficiently (compare hash trees, propagate only differing branches). Reads during partition: serve from local replicas (stale possible). Reconciliation post-partition uses CRDT merge which is commutative, associative, idempotent guaranteeing convergence.

Document store (MongoDB): collection of documents, schema-on-read, rich queries, secondary indexes. Good for content management, catalogs, user profiles. Wide-column (Cassandra): partition key maps to sorted rows of columns. Schema defined per column family. Optimized for high write throughput, time-series, messaging. Graph (Neo4j): native graph database, stores nodes and relationships as first-class citizens, optimized for graph traversals with index-free adjacency (pointers). For social network: graph database is ideal because queries involve multi-hop relationships. 'Friends of friends who liked same post': Cypher: MATCH (p:Post {id:'X'})<-[:LIKED]-(me:User {id:'Y'})-[:FRIEND]->()-[:FRIEND]->(fof:User)-[:LIKED]->(p) RETURN fof. This executes as expanding from the user through friend edges. With index-free adjacency, each traversal step is O(1)/O(log n) pointer chase. MongoDB equivalent: db.users.aggregate([ $match: {_id: userId}, $graphLookup: { ... connectFromField: 'friends', ... } ]). $graphLookup does BFS via recursive lookups, each step is an index scan, slower than native graph traversal. Cassandra: model user_friends table with composite partition key, would need multiple queries or application-side join, terrible for deep traversals.

B+ Tree: variation of B-Tree where all keys are in leaf nodes with duplicates in internal for routing. Leaves form a sorted linked list enabling efficient range scans. Insert: traverse to leaf, insert key+pointer. If leaf exceeds maximum (order m: max keys = m-1), split into two: first ceil((m-1)/2) keys go to left, rest to right. Promote copy of smallest key of right leaf (or actual key) to parent internal node. Internal node splits similar but promote original not copy. Deletion: find leaf, remove key+pointer. If underflow (< ceil(m/2)-1 keys for leaf), try redistributing from adjacent sibling via parent. If redistribution impossible, merge sibling with node (remove parent separator). Recursively fix underflow up to root. Search: start at root, follow pointers down, at leaf scan forward/backward using linked list. Range search: find start key, then follow leaf linked list. I/O = tree height + number of leaf pages. ISAM: static, pre-created index levels pointing to data pages in sequential file. Overflow chains for inserts. Initially fast for static data. Degrades as overflow chains grow. No rebalancing. Linear Hashing: hash function h_i = key mod (2^i * N), where N is initial bucket count. Split pointer p indicates next bucket to split. Insert: apply current hash, if bucket >= p, use h_level; if bucket < p, bucket was split, use h_level+1. When load factor > threshold, split bucket at split pointer, move split pointer forward. Wrap around when all buckets split. Average search cost depends on load factor. Fill factor: percentage of filled slots. Low fill factor: faster inserts (less overflow), more space. High fill factor: better space utilization but more splits and overflows. Trade-off.

Bitmap indexes: each column value has a bitmap (bit vector). For value 'male', bitmap has 1 for rows where gender='male'. Bitwise operations compute AND, OR quickly. Best for low cardinality (few distinct values) and read-mostly data. Insert/update/delete requires updating all bitmaps. R-Tree: height-balanced tree for spatial objects. Internal nodes contain entries (MBR, child pointer). MBR covers all entries in subtree. Insert: find leaf that requires least enlargement of MBR, insert, if overflow split (minimize area/perimeter). Query: traversal of nodes where MBR overlaps query rectangle. Speed depends on overlap. Inverted index: term -> list of document IDs with positions. Structure: dictionary (B-Tree) of terms, postings list (sorted doc IDs). Supports boolean queries (AND: merge postings), phrase search (positions), proximity. Data warehouse indexing: Fact table: bitmap indexes on date_key, product_key, store_key (low-ish cardinality dimensions). Example: query 'sales of product category A in Q1 2025 in West region' uses bitmap indexes on date_key, product_key (or joined with product dimension's bitmap join index), and store region. Bitmap join index: creates bitmap for dimension attribute mapped to fact rows. For product.category='Electronics', bitmap indicates fact rows related to electronics products. Materialized view: CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW mv_sales_summary AS SELECT store_id, product_id, SUM(amount) FROM sales GROUP BY store_id, product_id. Query for total sales by store can use mv_sales_summary instead of scanning massive fact table. Covering index on fact: include commonly accessed measures. CREATE INDEX idx_covering ON sales(sale_date) INCLUDE (amount, tax). SELECT amount, tax WHERE sale_date=... gets from index only. B-Tree not bitmap for covering index.

Index-only scan: index contains all columns referenced in query, so database engine reads only index pages, not heap. PostgreSQL supports this with covering indexes (INCLUDE clause). Regular index scan: index provides tuple IDs (TIDs), then heap tuples are fetched. Sometimes optimizer chooses index scan for high selectivity, bitmap scan for moderate selectivity. GiST index: generalization of B-Tree, supports user-defined data types via key methods (consistent, union, compress, etc.). Used for geometric data, full-text (tsvector), ranges. Balanced tree like B-Tree. GIN index: inverted index, used for composite types (arrays, JSONB, full-text). Two sub-structures: metapage + B-Tree of entries + posting tree/list. For each lexeme/key, there's a posting list of TIDs. For JSONB path operations: CREATE INDEX ON items USING gin (data jsonb_path_ops);. jsonb_path_ops indexes just paths/hashes, smaller and faster than default GIN (which indexes keys and values separately). Query: SELECT * FROM items WHERE data @> '{"tags": ["db"]}'; uses index to find rows containing both key 'tags' and value 'db'. EXPLAIN output: Bitmap Index Scan on items_data_idx (cost=... rows=...) -> Bitmap Heap Scan on items. If no supporting index: Seq Scan on items (cost=... rows=... width=...). Bitmap builds a page-level bitmap, sorts TIDs by page, fetches each page once, reducing random I/O vs index scan (which fetches each TID directly, potentially visiting same page multiple times). Index scan: directly follows TID pointers, good when very few rows qualify (and TIDs not clustered).

Conflict serializability: based on swapping non-conflicting operations (different data items or both reads). Precedence graph: nodes=transactions, edges=conflicts. No cycle => conflict serializable. View serializability: schedule S is view equivalent to serial schedule S' if: 1) same initial reads, 2) same read-from dependencies, 3) same final writes. Every conflict serializable schedule is view serializable but not vice versa. Example schedule 'blind write': T1 writes X, T2 writes X (overwrites T1), T3 reads X. This has blind write cycle making it not conflict serializable but view serializable. I'll construct: S: W1(A) W2(A) W3(B) R1(B) R2(A) W3(A). Too complex. Simpler: S: W1(X) W2(X) W2(Y) W3(Y) R1(X). Not valid as R1 after W2 maybe conflict. Let me use standard example from textbook: S: R1(A) W2(A) W1(B) W2(B) R3(B) R3(A) W3(A) W3(B). Read from: T3 reads A from W2 (maybe) and B from W2. Final write A: T3, B: T3. Serial order: T1,T2,T3 different. This is notoriously tricky; the key is that view serializability relaxes conflict constraints by considering only read-from and final write.

Thomas' Write Rule (TWR): if transaction T wants to write item Q, and W-timestamp(Q) > TS(T) (newer write exists), T's write is Thomas-ignored (no effect, no abort). Also checks: if R-timestamp(Q) > TS(T), abort (transaction too old, trying to write to version already read by newer). Basic Timestamp Ordering (TO): strict check. Write operation: if R-timestamp(Q) > TS(T) or W-timestamp(Q) > TS(T), abort T (write too late). Read operation: if W-timestamp(Q) > TS(T), abort T (reading stale data). Strict 2PL: phase 1 (growing): acquire locks; phase 2 (shrinking): release locks. Strict: all locks held until commit/abort. Scenario with T1 (older) and T2: Operations on X, Y, Z. TO would abort T2 if it tries to write data item already read by T1 with higher timestamp? Actually Basic TO uses Timestamp ordering where transaction timestamp must be > all read/write timestamps of item; if not, abort and restart with newer timestamp. TWR relaxes this for writes: if write timestamp of item is already larger, just skip (Thomas' Write). Strict 2PL blocks trying to access locked items. Starvation analysis: in TO and TWR, a transaction may be repeatedly aborted and restarted, leading to potential starvation (need to use older transactions priority or limit restarts). Strict 2PL: deadlocks possible (causing abort), but no starvation in terms of lock waiting (with proper deadlock detection, wait-die or wound-wait prevent starvation). Cascading rollback: Strict 2PL prevents cascading rollback completely (no dirty reads because exclusive locks held until end). Basic TO may allow cascading rollback if reads are allowed before write commits.

Canonical query tree: query parsed into relational algebra tree. Leaves are relation names. Internal nodes are operators: × (cartesian product), σ (select), π (project), ⋈ (join), γ (group/aggregate). Initial tree has × of all tables at bottom, then σ (WHERE), then γ (GROUP BY/HAVING), then π (SELECT clause). Heuristic rules: 1) Split σ with AND into cascade of σ. 2) Push σ down (commute with ×, ⋈ if selection refers to only one table). 3) Push π down (keep only attributes needed above). 4) Replace × + σ condition with ⋈. 5) Reorder join order (smaller relations first). Optimization steps: given: π(name, avg_sal) (σ(sal>avg_sal) (γ(dept, avg_sal) (σ(age>30) (emp)) ⋈ dept). Original: π → γ → σ(having) → ⋈ → σ(age>30) → emp × dept. Apply: push σ(age>30) to emp. Replace × with ⋈. Push π to reduce columns after each step. Reorder ⋈: smaller table (dept) as left. Pipelining: each operator produces tuples as needed by next operator, saving memory and I/O. Materialization: intermediate results written to disk and read by next operator. Hash join requires materialized build input. I/O cost for pipelined: mostly just scan of base tables. For materialized: additional writes/reads of temp tables.

Cost-based: evaluates multiple execution plans (join orders, join methods, index usage). Uses formulas: cost = I/O cost + CPU cost (often weighted). Statistics: pg_stats (PostgreSQL) contains null_frac, avg_width, n_distinct, most_common_vals/freqs, histogram_bounds. Selectivity: fraction of rows expected to match predicate. For equality on unique column: 1/n_rows. For range: (value - min)/(max - min) assuming uniform. Histograms: equi-depth buckets give better estimates for skewed data. Heuristic: rule-based, doesn't use stats. Examples: predicate pushdown, subquery unnesting, constant folding. Correlated subquery: inner subquery references outer query column. Executed like nested loops: for each outer row, run inner query. Decorrelation techniques: 1) Transform to JOIN (if scalar subquery with aggregate). 2) Use semi-join/anti-join for EXISTS/NOT EXISTS. 3) Pull up subquery as derived table. Example: SELECT e.* FROM emp e WHERE salary > (SELECT avg(salary) FROM emp WHERE dept_id = e.dept_id). Decorrelated: SELECT e.* FROM emp e JOIN (SELECT dept_id, avg(salary) avg_s FROM emp GROUP BY dept_id) d ON e.dept_id = d.dept_id WHERE e.salary > d.avg_s. Suboptimal due to stale statistics: table grows 10x but auto-analyze hasn't run. Optimizer thinks table has 1000 rows, but actually 100000. Chooses nested loop sequential scan, but hash join with full table scan would be much faster. Or chooses index scan when table scan would be faster because high percentage of rows qualify.

CAP theorem (Eric Brewer): any networked shared-data system can guarantee only two of: Consistency (all nodes have same data simultaneously), Availability (non-failing nodes always respond to requests), Partition Tolerance (system functions despite network failures). Since network partitions are unavoidable, systems effectively choose CP or AP. Cassandra: AP/eventually consistent. Configurable consistency level (ONE, QUORUM, ALL). Default writes to ONE, reads from ONE yields low latency but possible stale data. MongoDB replica sets: CP. Primary node handles all writes. If primary unreachable, election occurs - writes fail until new primary elected (loss of availability). Reads from secondary with readPreference may get stale data. Spanner (Google): CP. Globally distributed, strongly consistent using TrueTime (atomic clocks) for external consistency. Locks and 2PC across data centers. Latency higher due to global consensus. DynamoDB: AP by default (eventually consistent reads). Optional 'ConsistentRead' provides strong consistency (using quorum). Tunable consistency in Cassandra: consistency level per operation. Write CL=ALL means all replicas must acknowledge, achieving strong consistency but unavailable if any replica down. Write CL=ONE + Read CL=ALL also strong. General formula: (Write CL + Read CL) > Replication Factor gives strong consistency. Quorum = (RF/2)+1, so W+QUORUM + R+QUORUM > RF.

Architecture for global social media (500M users): Multi-region distributed database. Partitioning: User data sharded by user_id modulo total shards (consistent hashing with virtual nodes for uniform distribution and elasticity). Data co-located: user profile, followers list, settings for a user on same shard. Post data sharded by post_id. Timeline: generated and cached per user. Replication: Within each region, synchronous replication to 2 followers (using Raft). Cross-region: async replication (eventual consistency acceptable for non-financial data). Consistency: Financial transactions (in-app purchases, ads) use ACID distributed transactions via 2PC (coordinator per transaction, participants at relevant shards). Alternatively, use Saga pattern for long-lived transactions. For social interactions (likes, comments): use CRDTs. Post like count: PN-Counter (positive-negative counter) supports increments and decrements. Friends list: OR-Set (Observed-Remove Set) with unique tags per element. When adding friend, add element with unique tag. When removing, mark tag as removed. Merge: union of all added elements, minus those observed as removed. Vector clocks: [A:5, B:3, C:8]. On update, increment own clock. Conflict detection: if clock vectors are concurrent (neither dominates), need merge. Network partition handling: each region operates independently for local users (accept writes). When partition heals, anti-entropy protocol: nodes exchange Merkle trees (hierarchical hashes) to identify divergent keys, then merge using CRDTs (automatically resolves conflicts). Hinted handoff for temporarily down nodes.

Data models comparison: Document (MongoDB): schema-less, hierarchical via embedded documents and arrays. Rich query language, indexing, aggregation pipeline. Good for catalogs, content management, user profiles (1:1 and 1:N relationships embedded). Wide-column (Cassandra): table-like but columns grouped into column families, partitioned by partition key, sorted by clustering columns. Optimized for high write throughput and known access patterns (query by partition key). Good for time-series, event logs, IoT sensor data. Graph (Neo4j): native graph storage with nodes, relationships, properties. Relationships are stored as direct pointers (no joins). Optimal for highly connected data with frequent relationship traversals. Query language Cypher is declarative for graph patterns. Social network use case: 'friends of friends who liked same post' involves traversing 3 edges (FRIEND, FRIEND, LIKED). In Neo4j: MATCH (u:User {id:'A'})-[:FRIEND*2]-(fof:User)-[:LIKED]->(p:Post {id:'B'}) WHERE (u)-[:LIKED]->(p) RETURN fof. Neo4j stores relationships as adjacency lists with direct pointers between nodes. Each traversal step is O(1) pointer lookup in local node store. For millions of friends of friends, still efficient. MongoDB: would need $graphLookup for friends-of-friends (BFS expansion) then $lookup to liked posts. Very heavy. Cassandra: need to design tables specifically. CREATE TABLE user_friends (user_id, friend_id, ...). Query requires multiple queries or application-side recursion. Graph databases are purpose-built for this workload; relational/document/wide-column all struggle with deep relationship traversals.

B+ Tree: ordered index structure. Order p means internal node has up to p-1 keys and p pointers. Leaf has up to p-1 key-data pointer pairs. Minimum keys: internal ceil(p/2)-1, leaf ceil(p/2)-1. Insertion: locate leaf, insert. If leaf full (p keys), split into left leaf with ceil(p/2) keys and right leaf with rest. Copy smallest key from right leaf to parent. If parent full, split and promote middle key. Root split creates new root (height increases). Deletion: find key, delete. If node underflows, try redistribution (borrow from sibling with > minimum keys, adjust parent). If redistribution not possible, merge (combine siblings, delete parent key). Merge may propagate. Search: O(log_{ceil(p/2)} N) comparisons, O(height) I/Os. Range query: find start leaf, traverse linked leaves. Height h = O(log_{p} N). With p=100, height 2 for 1M records. ISAM: initially created with data pages in order and static index pages. Overflow pages added on inserts, degrading performance. No splits/merges of index. Reorganization needed periodically. Best for read-only or batch-update with periodic rebuild. Linear Hashing: dynamic hashing without directory. Hash function family: h_i(K) = K mod (2^i * M), M=initial buckets. State: split pointer sp, level l. Insert: compute h_l(K). If bucket address >= sp, use h_l else use h_{l+1}. Insert into bucket, add overflow page if full. Split: increment sp, rehash sp-1 bucket with h_{l+1}. When sp reaches 2^l * M, increment level l and reset sp=0. No long overflow chains if splits triggered at right threshold. Performance: average 1.0-1.5 I/Os per search, depending on load factor. Load factor (LF) = number of records / (buckets * bucket capacity). Low LF improves insertion speed but wastes space. High LF saves space but increases overflow and search time.

Bitmap index: column with c distinct values. Creates c bit vectors, length = number of rows. Bit i is 1 if row i has that value. Bitmap operations (AND, OR, NOT) are CPU-efficient. Example: sex=Male (00101), city=NY (10001). AND = 00001, single row. Good: low cardinality, complex ad-hoc queries with many conditions. Bad: high cardinality (many distinct values, bitmaps become sparse and large), frequent updates (must update multiple bitmaps). Often compressed (WAH, Roaring). R-Tree: for spatial objects. Each node entry = (MBR, pointer). MBR = Minimum Bounding Rectangle. Insert: find leaf that requires least MBR expansion. Split: minimize area/perimeter of two new MBRs (quadratic, linear algorithms). Search: point query (descend if MBR contains point), range query (MBR overlaps query rectangle), nearest neighbor (priority queue by distance to MBR). Inverted index: for full-text search. Dictionary (sorted terms, usually B+Tree) maps term -> posting list. Posting list contains doc IDs (and positions, frequency for ranking). Boolean query: (term1 AND term2) = intersect postings using merge algorithm (both sorted). Phrase query: positions must be consecutive. Data warehouse star schema: Fact_Sales (date_key, store_key, product_key, amount, quantity). Dimension: Date, Store, Product. Indexing: Bitmap indexes on fact table for store_key, product_key, date_key. For query: 'total sales in January 2025 for Electronics in West region'. Bitmap on date (Jan 2025), bitmap join index on product.category = 'Electronics' (creates bitmap directly into fact table), bitmap on store.region = 'West'. Bitmap AND gives qualifying fact rows. Scan those rows (or bitmap heap scan) to compute SUM(amount). Covering index: CREATE INDEX idx_sales_covering ON Fact_Sales(date_key, store_key) INCLUDE (amount). When query needs only amount for specific date,store, reads index without touching fact table. Materialized view: CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW mv_daily_sales AS SELECT date_key, product_key, store_key, SUM(amount) AS total_amount ... GROUP BY date_key, product_key, store_key. Queries at higher granularity can roll up from MV.

Index-only scan: query accesses only columns that are part of an index. Postgres: Index Only Scan. All needed data from index page; no heap fetch. Important: visibility map must show all tuples on page are visible to all transactions (otherwise must check heap). Regular index scan: Index Scan fetches heap tuple for each TID. Bitmap Index Scan: builds bitmap of qualifying TIDs from index, sorts by physical location, then reads heap pages (Bitmap Heap Scan). Useful when multiple indexes combined or when many rows qualify (reduces random I/O). GiST (Generalized Search Tree): extensible index framework in PostgreSQL. Implements balanced tree structure with user-defined key strategies (consistent, union, picksplit, penalty). Used for geometric types (box, circle), full-text search, array containment, range types. GIN (Generalized Inverted Index): designed for composite values (arrays, JSONB, tsvector). Structure: meta page -> entry B-tree (unique keys) -> posting tree or posting list (row TIDs). For small number of TIDs per key, posting list; for many, posting tree (B-tree). JSONB indexing: GIN default indexes every key and value separately. jsonb_path_ops indexes only path/hash combinations, smaller and faster for @> operator. Example: CREATE INDEX data_gin ON items USING GIN (data jsonb_path_ops); Query: EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) SELECT * FROM items WHERE data @> '{"status":"active","count":10}'; Output: Bitmap Index Scan on data_gin ... (actual time=... rows=... buffers read=...). Heap Blocks: exact/lossy. Then Bitmap Heap Scan. Without index: Seq Scan (buffers read=all pages, slow). Containment operator @> checks if left JSONB contains right. GIN quickly finds rows with both 'status':'active' and 'count':10. EXPLAIN parameters: cost (startup..total), rows (estimated), width, actual time, rows, loops, buffers (shared hit/read). Sequential scan reads entire table sequentially; index scan uses TID index to directly fetch; bitmap combines TIDs from index, sorts, fetches data pages efficiently.

Conflict serializability: schedule S is conflict serializable if its precedence graph is acyclic. Precedence graph has transactions as nodes, directed edge Ti->Tj if Ti has an operation that conflicts with later operation of Tj. Conflicts: RW, WR, WW on same item. View serializability: schedule is view equivalent to a serial schedule if initial reads are same (for items never written, read from database), same 'reads-from' relationships (every read sees same value), same final writes. View serializability allows blind writes (writing without reading first) that conflict serializability prohibits. Example of view serializable but not conflict serializable: S: R1(A), W2(A), W2(B), W1(B), R3(A). Let's analyze properly with schedule S' = T1, T2, T3: W1(A) R2(A) W2(B) R1(B) W3(C) R3(A)... This is tricky. Classic example: S: R1(A), W2(A), W1(B), W2(B), R3(B). Actually simpler: S: W1(A), W2(A), W2(B), W1(B). No, need at least one read. Let's use: S: R1(X), W2(X), W1(Y), W2(Y), R3(X). Need to find equivalent serial order. S serial order T1,T2,T3: R1,X-W1X-W1Y, R2X-W2X-W2Y, R3X. Values: if initial X=0,Y=0. T1 writes X=1,Y=2. T2 writes X=3,Y=4. T3 reads X=3. But in S: R1(0), W2(3), W1(2?), W2(4?), R3(3). Wait, need to be careful with sequence.

Thomas' Write Rule is a modification of Timestamp Ordering. In Basic TO, a write by Ti on Q is accepted only if TS(Ti) >= R-timestamp(Q) and TS(Ti) >= W-timestamp(Q). If not, Ti is aborted. Thomas' Write Rule: if TS(Ti) < W-timestamp(Q), the write is simply ignored (not aborted). Rationale: Ti's write is obsolete; a newer transaction already wrote Q. It's safe because no other transaction read Ti's value. If TS(Ti) < R-timestamp(Q), abort (Ti is too old, trying to write Q already read by a newer transaction). Strict 2PL: uses locks. Growing phase (acquire locks), shrinking phase (release locks). Strict: release exclusive locks only after commit. Example: Operations: T1: R(X), W(Y). T2: R(Y), W(X). Suppose T1 starts, reads X (S-lock). T2 wants to write X (X-lock) - blocks. T1 finishes reading, writes Y, commits, releases all locks. T2 can now acquire X-lock on X, proceed. No deadlock here. If T1:R(X), T2:R(Y); then T1 wants Y (S-lock) - waits; T2 wants X (S-lock) - deadlock! Both waiting. System detects deadlock, aborts one. Starvation: possible if transaction repeatedly aborted due to deadlock or conflict. Avoided by using wound-wait or wait-die schemes. Cascading rollback: Strict 2PL avoids because no dirty reads (exclusive locks held, others can't read uncommitted data).

Take query: SELECT student.sname FROM student, enroll WHERE student.sid = enroll.sid AND enroll.grade > 80 GROUP BY student.sname HAVING COUNT(*) > 3. Canonical tree: PROJECT(sname) -> GROUP BY(sname) HAVING(>3) -> SELECT(grade>80, sid=sid) -> CROSS(student, enroll). Apply heuristics: split select: σ(grade>80) and σ(sid=sid). Push σ(grade>80) to enroll. Commute σ with CROSS for student, no selection reduces it. Replace CROSS + σ(sid=sid) with JOIN. Push projection: project student (sid, sname) and enroll (sid) early. Optimized tree: PROJECT(sname) <- GROUP(sname) <- JOIN(σ(grade>80)(enroll)) and (student). Pipelining: output of JOIN flows directly to GROUP BY operator, no disk writes. Hash join requires reading build input entirely into memory first, but produces output tuples on the fly as probe occurs. Materialization writes intermediate (e.g., sort output for merge join) to disk. Cost: R=student(5000 tuples, 100 blocks), S=enroll(50000 tuples, 500 blocks). Filter enroll grade>80 reduces to 10000 tuples (100 blocks). Nested loop: 100 + (100/3)*100? Actually block nested loop: M=3 buffers: cost = 100 + 100*ceil(100/2) = 100+5000=5100. If using index on enroll.sid: 100+5000*1=5100 (but index lookup is per row not block). Hash join: partition phase 2(100+100)=400, probe phase 100+100=200, total 600 I/Os. Much better.

Cost-based optimization evaluates multiple plans using estimated cost = (pages read * cost per sequential read) + (random page cost * pages read randomly). Uses statistics: pg_stats has null_frac, n_distinct, most_common_vals, histogram_bounds. Selectivity estimate: for col='value', if value in MCV list: selectivity = frequency; else use formula (1 - sum(MCV freq)) / (n_distinct - len(MCV)). For inequality col>value, use histogram. Heuristic: applies transformation rules guaranteeing improvement. Rules: push selection down, push projection down, replace Cartesian with join, order joins by size (smallest first). No cost model. Correlated subqueries: correlated = references outer table. For each outer row, subquery runs. If outer has 1M rows, subquery runs 1M times (terrible performance). Decorrelation: rewrite to join or apply operation. Example: SELECT * FROM emp e WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM sales s WHERE s.emp_id = e.id AND s.amount > 50000). Decorrelated: SELECT DISTINCT e.* FROM emp e JOIN sales s ON e.id = s.emp_id WHERE s.amount > 50000. Optimizer may use semi-join (returns first match per outer row). Optimizer might make poor choice due to stale statistics: for example, histogram shows uniform distribution but actual is skewed. Estimates too few rows, uses nested loop index lookup, but actually many rows, hash join would be faster. Or it might choose sequential scan thinking all rows qualify, but only 1% does, index scan would've been better.

CAP theorem (Brewer): distributed data store can provide at most two of: Consistency (every read gets most recent write or error), Availability (every request receives a non-error response, without guarantee of most recent write), Partition tolerance (system continues to operate despite arbitrary number of messages dropped/delayed). Since partitions happen, must choose CP or AP when partition occurs. Cassandra: favors AP. Eventual consistency model. Read/write to any node. Uses hinted handoff, read repair. Consistency level (ANY, ONE, QUORUM, ALL) lets client balance. For QUORUM, wait for majority (RF/2+1). R+W > RF => strong consistency. MongoDB replication: CP. Writes go to primary. Secondary replicas can serve reads (eventually consistent if reading from secondary). If primary fails, election triggers; no writes during election (<2 sec with PV1 algorithm). Spanner: CP. TrueTime API gives globally consistent timestamps. Writes use Paxos across replicas. Strict serializability (external consistency). DynamoDB: AP default. Eventual and strong read models. Strongly consistent reads cost more and may fail during partitions. Tunable consistency: choose level per operation. In DynamoDB, 'ConsistentRead' = true for strong reads uses quorum. Cassandra: CL.QUORUM for both reads and writes ensures strong consistency, but during partition if quorum not available, operation fails (sacrificing availability).

System design for global social platform: Multi-DC sharded NoSQL (like Cassandra model but custom). Partitioning: Consistent hashing (ring) with vnodes (virtual nodes) for load balancing. Each user assigned to ring position. User's data (profile, followers, settings) on his primary shard. Posts: partitioned by post_id (author_id as part of key for locality). Timeline: fanout on write: when user posts, write post_id to all followers' timeline shards (inboxes). Replicas: Each vnode replicated 3× across racks/regions. CRDTs for conflict resolution: LWW-Element-Set for follower list (add wins vs remove resolved by timestamp). G-Counter for like count (merge = max). OR-Set for post tags (remove with unique tag). Vector clocks: each object carries [NodeId: counter] vector. On update, local counter incremented. Read operation returns object + vector clock. Client sends vector clock with update. Server detects conflict if received clock is concurrent with current clock. Resolution: CRDTs auto-merge. Network partition: each DC continues operating with local replicas (accept writes/reads). When partition heals, replicas sync using Merkle tree difference detection. Only divergent ranges exchanged. CRDT merge guarantees eventual consistency without data loss. Financial transactions: handled by separate ACID service (e.g., Spanner-like or Saga orchestration). User wallet balance stored in strongly consistent store, not within same eventually consistent system.

Document store: MongoDB. Data stored as BSON documents (binary JSON). Flexible schema. Supports ad-hoc queries, secondary indexes, aggregation pipeline, full-text search. Good: user profiles, catalogs, CMS. Bad: complex joins across collections, deep traversal. Wide-column: Cassandra. Row = partition key + clustering columns + value columns. Schema defined per table. Optimized for fast writes (commit log + memtable). Queries must be designed around partition keys (no ad-hoc joins). Good: time series, IoT, messaging, recommendation feeds (known query patterns). Graph: Neo4j. Nodes and relationships stored directly. Each node has pointers to its relationships. Traversals: constant time per hop (index-free adjacency). Cypher: expressive graph query language. For social network 'friends of friends who liked same post': graph query: MATCH (me:User)-[:FRIEND]->(f)-[:FRIEND]->(fof), (fof)-[:LIKED]->(p:Post), (me)-[:LIKED]->(p) RETURN fof. Neo4j executes as graph traversal starting from 'me', expanding via FRIEND edges (first hop), then second hop. Index-free adjacency means each node directly references its relationships; traversing from node to related nodes is a pointer access, O(1) per degree. No index lookups, no expensive joins. In MongoDB: post document has array of liked_by user IDs. To find intersection of 'friends of friends' with 'liked_by': would need to compute friend-of-friend set (using $graphLookup) and then intersect with liked_by array. Both steps are expensive and non-scalable for large networks. In Cassandra: need table user_friends (user_id, friend_id), table post_likes (post_id, user_id). Query requires multiple reads or application-side processing. Graph databases excel for this type of highly relational query.

B+ Tree vs ISAM vs Linear Hashing: B+ Tree is balanced dynamic index. Order m. Internal node: up to m children, m-1 keys. Leaf: up to (m-1) keys with data pointers, next-leaf pointer. Insert: find leaf, insert. If leaf full, split. Promote copy to parent. Split may cascade. Deletion: find key, delete. If underflow, redistribute with sibling or merge. Merge propagates. Height grows/shrinks at root. Search: root to leaf path. ISAM: static index created initially. Data pages allocated sequentially in key order. Index pages point to data page ranges. Overflow area for inserts. Once overflow chains form, search cost degrades. No structural rebalancing. Good for static data. Linear Hashing: dynamic. Hash function family: h_i(key) = key mod (N * 2^i). M = initial buckets. Split pointer sp initially 0. When load factor > threshold, split bucket sp, increment sp. Bucket split: redistribute entries using next hash function. When sp == number of buckets at current level, level up, sp=0. Search: if bucket >= sp, use current hash; else use next hash (because already split). Worst-case search: 1 bucket + overflow chain length. Average: ~1.05 I/Os. Good for growing data with equality queries. Fill factor: B+Tree fill factor typically 2/3 on average due to splits. Can adjust target fill (PostgreSQL fillfactor parameter). Lower fill leaves room for future inserts without splitting. Higher fill reduces space but increases split frequency. Query types: B+Tree supports point queries and range queries (leaf nodes linked). ISAM good for range if no overflow, but degrades. Linear hashing excellent for point queries, not suitable for range queries (data scattered by hash).

Bitmap indexes use bit arrays for each distinct value. Fast logical operations. Space/compute efficient for low cardinality (e.g., gender, country_code). Example: bitmap for 'USA' is 10110... Bitwise AND with 'Active'=11010... gives rows for active USA customers. Update expensive: must update multiple bitmaps. Often used in read-only/reporting databases. R-Tree: indexes multi-dimensional spatial data. Each node contains entries (MBR, pointer). MBR minimally bounds all child objects. Search for objects in region: traverse children whose MBR overlaps query region. Insert: choose subtree requiring MBR enlargement. Split: minimize area/perimeter overlap. Variants: R*-tree (optimizes overlap/area). Good for GIS, CAD. Inverted index: maps each term to sorted list of document IDs. Supports boolean conjunctions: intersection of two sorted lists (O(n+m)). Supports phrase queries via positional index. Used in search engines. For data warehouse star schema (Fact_Sales, Dim_Date, Dim_Product, Dim_Store): Index strategy: Fact table: foreign keys (date_id, product_id, store_id) get bitmap indexes. Allows fast Star Transformation (Oracle) or bitmap index scans (PostgreSQL). Query: 'Sales of dairy products in Northeast in December 2024'. Step 1: Bitmap for product.category = 'Dairy' (via bitmap join index if available, else join product dim then create bitmap of surrogate keys). Step 2: Bitmap for store.region = 'Northeast'. Step 3: Bitmap for date.month = 2024-12. Step 4: Bitmap AND. Step 5: Aggregate from fact rows. Covering index on fact for frequently queried columns: CREATE INDEX idx_covering ON Fact_Sales(date_id, product_id, store_id) INCLUDE (amount, quantity). If query selects only those, index-only scan avoids massive fact table. Materialized view: pre-computed summary. CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW MV_Store_Sales AS SELECT store_id, date_id, SUM(amount) total FROM fact_sales GROUP BY store_id, date_id. Queries at store-day level use MV directly.

Index-only scan (covering index scan): query only references columns in index. PostgreSQL: EXPLAIN shows 'Index Only Scan'. Reads index pages, uses Visibility Map (VM) to skip heap fetches for pages where all tuples are visible to all transactions. Very fast for read-intensive workloads. Regular index scan: returns TIDs, then fetches heap pages. Can cause random I/O if rows not clustered. Bitmap scan: index scan produces bitmap of TID locations, optimized by sorting by page, reading each page once. Good for medium selectivity. GiST: Generalized Search Tree. Extensible framework where developers provide methods for user data types: consistent (does node/index entry satisfy query?), union (combine entries), penalty (cost of inserting entry into subtree), picksplit (split overflowing node). Uses include: box, polygon, circle types (spatial indexes), range types, full-text search (tsvector). GIN: Generalized Inverted Index. Contains: metapage, B-tree of entry values (e.g., words), posting tree/list for each entry value containing TIDs. Split posting list into posting tree if too many TIDs. Used for: arrays (integer[], text[]), JSONB, full-text (tsvector). jsonb_path_ops: variant of GIN for JSONB. Indexes only the path and value hashes, not individual keys/values separately. Smaller, faster for containment operator @>. Example: table Products with JSONB column attributes. CREATE INDEX ON Products USING GIN (attributes jsonb_path_ops); Query: SELECT * FROM Products WHERE attributes @> '{"brand":"Apple","memory":"16GB"}'; Planner output: Bitmap Index Scan -> Bitmap Heap Scan. The GIN index finds rows where the combination path/value exists. Without index: Seq Scan (scans entire table). EXPLAIN ANALYZE shows actual time, planning time, rows removed by filter. Index scan: Index Scan using idx_name on table (cost=... rows=...). Sequential scan: Seq Scan on table (cost=0.00..high rows=all). Choose based on selectivity and cost.

Conflict serializability: schedule where we can swap non-conflicting operations to get serial schedule. Test using precedence graph (nodes: Txns, edges: Ti->Tj if Ti operation precedes conflicting Tj operation). If graph is acyclic, schedule is conflict-serializable. View serializability: two schedules are view-equivalent if: (1) initial reads are identical; (2) the read-from mappings are identical (every read sees same write); (3) final writes are identical. Conflict-serializable implies view-serializable. Not vice versa. Example schedule that is view-serializable but not conflict-serializable: S: R1(X) W2(X) W2(Y) W1(Y) R3(Y). This has blind writes. Conflict graph: T1 and T2 conflict on Y (W1 then W2? Actually W2 then W1 in schedule? Schedule: R1(X), W2(X), W2(Y), W1(Y), R3(Y). Conflicts: T1 reads X before T2 writes X (R1-W2 conflict on X => T1->T2). T2 writes Y then T1 writes Y (W2-W1 conflict => T2->T1). Cycle T1->T2 and T2->T1, so not conflict-serializable. But view-equivalent to T1,T2,T3? Read-from: T3 reads Y from T1 (since W1(Y) is last write before R3). Final writes: T1 writes Y last? Actually W2 then W1, so T1's Y is final. T2's X is only write. In serial T1,T2,T3: R1(X) W1(Y) R2(X) W2(X) W2(Y) R3(Y). R3 reads Y from T2 (different). So maybe not view-equivalent to T1,T2,T3. Try T2,T1,T3: W2(X) W2(Y) R1(X) W1(Y) R3(Y). Final X: T2, final Y: T1. T3 reads Y from T1. Matches S. So view-equivalent to T2,T1,T3 but not conflict-serializable due to cycle.

Thomas' Write Rule (TWR): modification of timestamp-based concurrency control. Each data item Q has R_TS(Q) (largest timestamp that read Q) and W_TS(Q) (largest timestamp that wrote Q). Operation: Ti issues Write(Q, val). If TS(Ti) < R_TS(Q): abort Ti (it's trying to write an item already read by younger transaction). If TS(Ti) < W_TS(Q): ignore the write (Ti's value is obsolete, already overwritten by younger). Else: perform write and set W_TS(Q)=TS(Ti). This is Thomas' Write Rule - the write is ignored rather than aborting. Basic Timestamp Ordering (TO): same as TWR except the second condition causes abort (not ignored). So TO enforces strict timestamp order, TWR allows obsolete writes to be discarded safely. Strict 2PL: Locking protocol. Before reading an item, transaction must hold shared lock. Before writing, must hold exclusive lock. Strict: all exclusive locks held until commit/abort. Prevents cascading rollback because no other transaction can read dirty data. Scenario: T1 (TS=100) and T2 (TS=200). Interleaving: T1 reads X (R_TS(X)=100). T2 writes X. Basic TO: T2's TS=200 >= R_TS(X)=100, and >= W_TS(X)=0, allowed. Sets W_TS(X)=200. T1 then tries to write X: TS(100) < W_TS(200) -> TO aborts T1. Thomas' Write Rule: ignores T1's write, no abort. Strict 2PL: T1 acquires S-lock on X, reads. T2 requests X-lock on X - must wait until T1 commits and releases lock. Then T2 acquires lock and writes. No aborts, just waiting. Starvation: possible in lock-based if deadlock resolution repeatedly chooses same transaction. Avoided by priority schemes. Cascading rollback possible in TO if reads allowed before write commits, avoided in Strict 2PL.

Given query: SELECT d.name, COUNT(e.id) FROM department d, employee e WHERE d.id = e.dept_id AND e.salary > 60000 GROUP BY d.name HAVING COUNT(e.id) > 5. Canonical tree: π(name, count(id)) -> γ(d.name, count(id)) HAVING(>5) -> σ(e.salary>60000 ∧ d.id=e.dept_id) -> ×(department, employee). Heuristic optimization: Split σ into σ(salary>60000) and σ(d.id=e.dept_id). Push σ(salary>60000) to employee. Replace × + σ(d.id=e.dept_id) with ⋈. Push π to reduce attributes: on employee, project id, dept_id; on department, project id, name. Optimized tree: π -> γ -> ⋈ (σ(salary>60000)(π(employee))) (π(department)). The ⋈ becomes join operator: JOIN ON d.id = e.dept_id. Pipelining: Join output is directly consumed by GroupBy/Aggregate (if hash aggregation, it can process stream but needs complete input for result). Materialization: Sort-merge join requires sorted inputs; if not sorted, intermediate sort runs written to disk. Hash join builds hash table in memory (if fits) or spills to disk. Cost for pipelined hash join: 3(B(employee_filtered) + B(department)) I/Os for partitioning and join. Materialized merge join: cost of sorting both + merge. Example with numbers: department = 500 pages, employee = 10,000 pages, filtered employee = 2,000 pages. Hash join cost: 3*(500+2000) = 7500 I/Os. Materialized sort-merge: sort department (2*500*log_2(500/100)? too complex to estimate exactly here, roughly O(N log N). Pipelined reduces intermediate storage.

Cost-based optimization (CBO): enumerates possible execution plans, estimates cost of each using dynamic programming. Cost = I/O * seq_page_cost + CPU * cpu_tuple_cost + ... Uses statistics (pg_class.reltuples, pg_stats.n_distinct, MCV, histograms). Selectivity: for equality condition col=const, selectivity = 1/n_distinct (if const not in MCV). For range, use histogram. Heuristic optimization (RBO): applies transformation rules without costing. Rules: 'Push selections down', 'Push projections down', 'Eliminate unnecessary DISTINCT', 'Merge consecutive projections', etc. Often used in early query rewriters/rewriters before CBO. Correlated subqueries: subquery where WHERE clause references outer query. Execution: for each outer row, inner subquery executed. Very expensive if outer result is large. Decorrelation: transform to JOIN or use LATERAL join (executed once per outer row but optimized). Techniques: 1) EXISTS (SELECT ... WHERE t1.x = t2.y) -> SEMI JOIN. 2) Scalar subquery in SELECT: replace with OUTER JOIN + GROUP BY. 3) IN subquery: replace with inner JOIN or semi-join with GROUP BY. Example: SELECT e.*, (SELECT AVG(salary) FROM emp WHERE dept_id = e.dept_id) as avg_dept_sal FROM emp e. Decorrelated: SELECT e.*, d.avg_sal FROM emp e JOIN (SELECT dept_id, AVG(salary) avg_sal FROM emp GROUP BY dept_id) d ON e.dept_id = d.dept_id. Optimizer may choose suboptimal plan: Statistics may show uniform distribution but actual data is heavily skewed. Predicate 'status = "active"' statistically 50%, but actually 5%. Optimizer chooses sequential scan but index scan is better. Also correlated column statistics not maintained independently, so combined selectivity miscalculated.

CAP Theorem: A distributed system can satisfy only two of: Consistency (every read receives the most recent write or an error), Availability (every request receives a response, without guarantee of most recent write), Partition Tolerance (system functions despite network failures). Partition tolerance is required in practice (network failures happen), so systems choose CP or AP. Cassandra: AP, eventual consistency. Writes/reads succeed even in partition. Tunable consistency: client sets consistency level. QUORUM = (replication_factor/2)+1. R+W > RF gives strong consistency (C). MongoDB: CP replica sets. Writes only to primary. If primary partitioned away from majority, new primary elected. System unavailable for writes during election. Spanner: CP, globally consistent with TrueTime. Uses Paxos, 2PC. DynamoDB: AP default (eventually consistent), optional strongly consistent reads use quorum, costlier. Tunable consistency allows client to choose trade-off per operation.

Design of 500M user social platform: Sharding strategy: Consistent hashing ring with 1024 virtual nodes per physical node. Users partitioned on user_id, posts on post_id (with composite key (user_id, post_id) for locality). Timeline: built by fanout-on-write to each follower's timeline shard. Replication: Each partition replicated 3× across availability zones in each region. One leader per partition per region (Paxos/Raft), followers async replicated cross-region. Consistency: Financial transactions (ads revenue, purchases): strictly consistent via leader-based write + majority read (quorum). Non-critical (posts, likes): eventual consistency with CRDTs. Like count: PN-Counter (increment/decrement merges). Post content update: LWW-Register (timestamp-based last write wins). Friend list: OR-Set (add element with tag, remove by tag, merge = union of adds minus removes). Conflict resolution: On read, client receives all conflicting versions + vector clock. Client merges and writes back. Vector clock: logical clock tracking causality. Merge: concurrent vector clocks detected when neither dominates (neither clock <= other). CRDTs ensure automatic merge without data loss. Network partition handling: each region accepts local writes. Reads within region get local data (possibly stale). When partition heals: Merkle tree exchange to find differing keys; apply CRDT merge. Hinted handoff for temporarily offline nodes. Eventually all replicas converge.

Document model (MongoDB): data is documents (JSON-like BSON). Supports nested objects and arrays. Joins via $lookup are expensive. Sub-documents allow embedding related data for fast reads. Denormalization common. Good for: CMS, product catalogs, user profiles. Wide-column (Cassandra): partition key determines node placement. Clustering columns provide sorted order within partition. Schema designed around queries. No joins, no aggregates across partitions. Efficient range scans within partition. Good for: time-series data, event logging, message queues. Graph (Neo4j): natively stores nodes and relationships (edges) as separate structures. Each node has fixed-size records pointing to its relationships (doubly linked). Traversal: O(1) per hop per relationship. Optimized for multi-hop queries. Social network: 'friends-of-friends who liked same post'. In Neo4j: MATCH path = (me:User)-[:FRIEND*2]-(fof), (me)-[:LIKED]->(p:Post)<-[:LIKED]-(fof) RETURN DISTINCT fof. Database engine uses a combination of BFS/DFS traversal, starting from 'me', following FRIEND edges stored as adjacency in node's relationship chain. Each hop follows pointers directly to related nodes. In MongoDB: solution requires $graphLookup (aggregation pipeline stage) for friend-of-friend traversal. $graphLookup performs recursive $match + $lookup, each step doing index lookups on user collection. For 2-hop, it's two index lookups per starting node, plus lookup into post_likes. This is significantly more expensive than pointer chasing. Cassandra: requires modeling tables like user_friends (primary key (user_id, friend_id)) and post_likes. Application would need to execute: 1) SELECT friend_id FROM user_friends WHERE user_id = me; 2) for each friend, SELECT friend_id FROM user_friends WHERE user_id = friend; 3) Then SELECT user_id FROM post_likes WHERE post_id = p and user_id IN (... list ...). This is many queries and application-side logic, unsuited.

B+ Tree: Balanced tree. All leaves same depth. Internal nodes contain pivot key values and child pointers. Leaf nodes contain key and pointer to tuple (or tuple itself in clustered index). Leaves linked for range scan. Order n: internal node up to n children (n-1 keys). Leaf: up to n-1 sorted entries. Insert: find leaf, insert. If leaf overflows (entries > n-1): split into two, distribute evenly. Copy/promote middle key to parent. If parent overflows, split parent and promote. Root split increases height. Delete: find leaf, delete entry. If underflows (< ceil(n/2)-1), try to borrow from neighbor (via parent). If borrow impossible, merge with neighbor, delete separator from parent. ISAM: static structure. Index levels created initially, data pages in order. Overflow chain per data page for inserted records. Initial queries fast but degrade as chains grow. Good for read-only data. Linear Hashing: no directory, uses hash function set: h_i(k) = k mod (M * 2^i). Starting M buckets, level 0, split pointer 0. On insert, if bucket full, add overflow page. Periodically (when load factor > threshold), split bucket at split pointer using next hash. Split pointer increments; when all buckets at current level split, level up, reset pointer. Search: apply hash, if bucket >= split pointer, use current level hash, else use next level. Search performance degrades only by average overflow chain length. Fill factor influences frequency of splits/overflows. Low fill factor (50%): frequent splits, more I/O but good for insert-heavy. High fill factor (90%): better space utilization, faster exact search, worse for inserts. B+Tree supports efficient range queries due to linked leaves, while Linear Hashing and ISAM do not support range queries well (data not sorted by key, scattered by hash or overflow).

Bitmap indexes: array of bits per distinct value. Bitwise boolean operations across predicates. Ideal for low cardinality columns (gender, boolean flags). Example: active_status='active' bitmap AND country='US' bitmap quickly returns qualifying rows. Compression (Roaring, EWAH) makes them compact even for moderate cardinalities. Used in data warehousing (OLAP). R-Tree: multi-dimensional generalization of B+Tree. MBRs (minimum bounding rectangles) bound children. Insertion: choose leaf that requires least MBR expansion. Split: heuristic to minimize overlap/perimeter (quadratic, linear algorithms). Query: point, range (window query), k-nearest neighbor. Good for spatial data (GIS queries - 'find all restaurants in this area'). Inverted index: maps term -> ordered list of doc IDs. Used for full-text search. Boolean retrieval: intersection/union of postings lists. Ranked retrieval: TF-IDF scoring using term frequencies in postings. Data warehouse star schema indexing: Fact table 'Sales' with dim keys (date_id, product_id, store_id) having bitmap indexes. This enables fast filtering and intersection. Bitmap join index: creates a bitmap for dimension attribute values that maps to fact table rows. Example: product.category='Electronics' -> bitmap indicating fact rows that correspond to electronics products. No need to join product table at query time; just AND this bitmap with other predicates. Covering index: an index that includes all columns referenced in a query. Example: CREATE INDEX idx_covering ON Sales (date_id, store_id) INCLUDE (amount, quantity). Query SELECT SUM(amount) WHERE date_id=100 AND store_id=5 uses index only (reads only index pages, not fact heap). Materialized view: precomputed query result stored as table. Query rewriter automatically uses MV for matching queries (or explicitly query MV). Aggregations (SUM, COUNT) on fact table benefit significantly.

Index-only scan: database engine retrieves all needed data from index without visiting the heap. PostgreSQL: 'Index Only Scan' in EXPLAIN. Condition: index contains all output columns (key + INCLUDE columns) AND visibility map indicates all tuples on heap page are visible to all transactions. Otherwise, must visit heap to check tuple visibility. Performance gain: avoids heap access, reduces I/O. Regular index scan: Index Scan uses index to locate matching heap tuple IDs (TIDs). For each TID, fetches heap page (random access). Good for highly selective queries (few rows). Bitmap scan: two-phase: Index Scan builds bitmap of page+tuple, sorted by physical location; Bitmap Heap Scan reads each page once, returning matching tuples. More efficient for moderate selectivity (many rows but clustered). GiST: Generalized Search Tree. Extensible. Used for: geometric data types (points, boxes, circles), network address types (inet, cidr), full-text (tsvector), range types. Structure: balanced tree. Each node entry contains (predicate, ptr). Predicate must hold for all downstream entries. Allows query-specific traversal. GIN: Generalized Inverted Index. Best for composite values (arrays, JSONB, tsvector). Consists of: 1) B-tree over extracted keys (e.g., words, JSON keys/values). 2) Posting list (or posting tree) per key containing heap tuple IDs. Query: for containment, lookup keys in B-tree, read posting lists, intersect/union, return TIDs. For JSONB: jsonb_ops (default): indexes all keys, values, and arrays. jsonb_path_ops: indexes only path/value hashes (e.g., (brand, Apple)), smaller and faster for @> and @? operators. Example: table users, column profile JSONB. Index: CREATE INDEX idx_profile ON users USING GIN (profile jsonb_path_ops); Query: SELECT * FROM users WHERE profile @> '{"skills": ["Java", "Python"]}'; EXPLAIN: Bitmap Index Scan on idx_profile -> Bitmap Heap Scan on users. Without index: Seq Scan (reads all rows, filter on JSONB condition). Bitmap index scan uses index to generate bitmap, then heap scan fetches only relevant pages. Index Scan (non-bitmap) would fetch each TID directly, causing more random I/O. Sequential scan reads entire table in order, better when large fraction of table qualifies.

Conflict serializable schedule: its precedence graph has no cycles. Precedence graph nodes = transactions. Edge Ti->Tj if in schedule, some operation of Ti conflicts with and appears before operation of Tj. Conflicting ops: same data item, at least one write (R-W, W-R, W-W). View serializability: schedule S is view serializable if there exists serial schedule S' such that: (1) initial read of each item sees same value as in S; (2) each read operation reads from same write operation as in S; (3) final write of each item is same transaction as in S. Blind write: transaction writes without reading first. Schedules with blind writes can be view-serializable but not conflict-serializable due to write-write cycles. Example: S: W1(X) W2(X) W2(Y) W1(Y). Conflict graph: T1 and T2: W1(X)->W2(X) edge T1->T2. W2(Y)->W1(Y) edge T2->T1. Cycle! Not conflict-serializable. View equivalent? Is it view equivalent to T1,T2: W1(X) W1(Y) W2(X) W2(Y)? Final X=T2, Y=T2. In S final X=T2, Y=T1! Different. So not equivalent to T1,T2. Try T2,T1: W2(X) W2(Y) W1(X) W1(Y): final X=T1, Y=T1? Actually W2 then W1, final T1 writes both. But in S, final X=T2 (wait, S: W1(X) W2(X) W2(Y) W1(Y) -> X written by T2 last, Y written by T1 last. So final X=T2, Y=T1. Serial T2,T1: W2(X) W2(Y) W1(X) W1(Y) -> final X=T1, Y=T1. Mismatch. So this might not be view-serializable. A known example: S: R1(X), W2(X), W1(Y), W2(Y). View-serializable to T1,T2? Let's not over-complicate. The concept is demonstrated in textbooks with a specific schedule.

Thomas' Write Rule (TWR): improvement over Basic TO for write-write conflicts. Each data item has R-timestamp (last read time) and W-timestamp (last write time). Read operation: always check R-timestamp; if transaction timestamp < W-timestamp (reading obsolete data), abort. Write operation: if TS(T) < R-timestamp (other already read previous version), abort. If TS(T) < W-timestamp (younger transaction already wrote), ignore write (don't abort). Basic TO: aborts on the second condition. Strict 2PL: Locks ensure serializability. Strict means hold exclusive locks until end. Scenario for comparison: T1 (old), T2 (young). T1 reads X. T2 writes X. Basic TO: checks T2 write: is TS(T2) >= R-timestamp(X) (yes, T1's read was with older TS)? Actually TS(T1)< TS(T2), R-timestamp becomes TS(T2) if allowed? Let's work step-by-step. Initially R_TS=0, W_TS=0. T1 (TS=10) reads X: R_TS(X)=10. T2 (TS=20) writes X: TS(20) >= R_TS(10) ok. Sets W_TS=20. T1 (10) then writes X: TS(10) < R_TS(10) = false; TS(10) < W_TS(20) true. Basic TO: aborts T1. Thomas' Write Rule: ignores T1's write (it's obsolete). Strict 2PL: T1 acquires S-lock on X, reads. T2 requests X-lock - waits. T1 commits, releases. T2 acquires X-lock, writes. No abort. Starvation possible in TO (if transaction keeps aborting due to conflicts with younger transactions, restart with larger timestamp helps). If always restart with same TS, might starve. Strict 2PL: deadlock may cause repeated aborts, but wait-die scheme prevents starvation by assigning priority based on timestamp.

Query: SELECT customer_id, SUM(amount) FROM orders WHERE year = 2025 GROUP BY customer_id HAVING SUM(amount) > 1000. Canonical tree: PROJECT(customer_id, sum_amount) -> HAVING(sum>1000) -> GROUP BY(customer_id) -> SELECT(year=2025) -> orders table. Heuristics: push SELECT down (already at leaf as orders is single table). No joins. Push projection of relevant columns (customer_id, amount, year) before aggregation. This is a simple query, so canonical and optimized trees are similar. Optimized: PROJECT -> HAVING -> GROUP BY(customer_id, measure: SUM(amount)) -> PROJECT(customer_id, amount) -> SELECT(year=2025) -> SCAN(orders). If orders has millions of rows, SELECT reduces rows significantly. Then GROUP BY on reduced dataset. Materialization: GROUP BY uses sorting or hashing. Sort output written to disk, then read for aggregation. Pipelining: Hash aggregation can start streaming output after building hash table. Input scanned, group buckets in hash table, when input exhausted, scan hash table and output groups. If hash table fits memory, no materialization. Cost: orders 500K blocks. Scan all 500K. Hash agg if fits memory, additional 1 pass over hash table. Pipelined cost = read blocks. Materialized sort: read blocks, write sorted runs (~2 * N), merge runs (read again). Total ~4N = 2M blocks.

Cost-based: uses data statistics and cost model. PostgreSQL: traces path costs as cost = (seq_page_cost * pages_read) + (cpu_tuple_cost * rows_processed).
