Statistics analyzer (ANALYZE) maintains pg_class (relpages, reltuples) and pg_stats (n_distinct, most_common_vals, histogram_bounds, correlation). Selectivity = estimated fraction of rows matching condition. Multiply by total rows for cardinality. Heuristic: rule-based. Transform relational algebra expression using heuristic rules without cost evaluation. 'Push down selections' always reduces cardinality so beneficial. 'Push down projections' reduces row width. Correlated subqueries are inefficient because inner loop executed for each outer row. Optimizers use query rewriting to decorrelate. Example: SELECT * FROM orders o WHERE o.total > (SELECT AVG(ord.total) FROM orders ord WHERE ord.customer_id = o.customer_id). Decorrelate: create derived table avg_orders (customer_id, avg_total) = SELECT customer_id, AVG(total) FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id. Then: SELECT o.* FROM orders o JOIN avg_orders a ON o.customer_id = a.customer_id WHERE o.total > a.avg_total. Suboptimal plan example: data with many NULLs in indexed column. Statistics show n_distinct=1000 but actually only 10 non-null distinct values out of 1M rows. Selectivity estimate for IS NULL is wrong (default 0.5? no NULL fraction from stats). Index on that column chosen but sequential scan better.

CAP theorem: Distributed data system characteristics - Consistency, Availability, Partition tolerance. Only 2 of 3 achievable simultaneously. Cassandra (AP): tunable consistency from eventual to strong. Default: write to one, read from one = eventual. With QUORUM, strong consistency but if partition, quorum unreachable -> operation fails (CP mode). MongoDB replica set (CP): primary for writes. If primary partitioned, majority elects new primary, old primary can't serve writes (availability sacrificed). Spanner (CP): strong external consistency using TrueTime and Paxos. Available as long as quorum reachable. DynamoDB (AP default): eventually consistent reads, optional strongly consistent. Tunable consistency: key feature of Dynamo/Cassandra. Client can specify number of replicas to read/write. W + R > N ensures strong consistency. Example: N=3, W=2, R=2 => overlap of at least 1 replica, returning latest write. If partition isolates one replica, W=2 not met -> write fails (availability sacrificed). If W=1, R=3, write succeeds always (AP) but read may fail if 3 not reachable.

Design for 500M user platform: Use multiple geographically distributed data centers. Partitioning: consistent hashing ring across clusters. Users: userID hash. Posts: postID hash. User timeline: list of postIDs (sharded by userID). Replication: each partition replicated 3 times (1 leader, 2 followers per region). Multi-leader across regions (conflict resolution needed). Consistency: financial transactions (in-app purchase): strong consistency needed. Route financial operations to dedicated service (e.g., stripe-like, or use ACID RDBMS with cross-shard 2PC). For social data: CRDTs. Like counter: GCounter (merge = max). Friend list: 2P-Set (two-phase set: added elements set, removed elements set; element must be in added and not in removed). Advantage: simple, converges. Disadvantage: removed element cannot be re-added (tombstone issue). So OR-set is better. Vector clocks: identify causal relationships. If clock A = [1,5] and B = [3,0], they are concurrent (neither dominates). Conflict resolution: LWW (last-writer-wins) by timestamp if semantics allow; otherwise merge sets. Network partition: each DC keeps accepting writes. Sync via Merkle trees periodically (or anti-entropy). When syncing, apply CRDT merge to resolve divergent data. For financial data, block writes if quorum lost (use Raft/Paxos).

Document (MongoDB): collection of documents (BSON). Schema flexibility. Embedding related data (e.g., comments within post document) reduces joins. Good for: blog, e-commerce catalog, user profiles. Wide-column (Cassandra): rows with varying columns, grouped into column families. Partition key for distribution, clustering columns for sort. Query by partition key is very fast. Good for: sensor data (partition by device_id, cluster by timestamp), messaging (partition by user_id, cluster by message_id). Graph (Neo4j): nodes and edges stored natively. Relationships stored as doubly-linked lists on node. Traversal is pointer chasing: O(1) per relationship expanded. For 'friends of friends who liked same post': Cypher: MATCH (u:User {id:'me'})-[:FRIEND*2]-(fof:User), (u)-[:LIKED]->(p:Post)<-[:LIKED]-(fof) RETURN fof. Neo4j starts at node 'me', follows FRIEND relationships (first hop = direct friends, second hop = friends-of-friends). Each relationship traversal is an O(1) pointer dereference from the current node's relationship chain. Then from each fof, checks if edge LIKED to p exists, also O(1). In MongoDB: use aggregation pipeline: $match user, $graphLookup to get friends-of-friends, then $lookup to liked posts collection, then $match to filter those who liked the same post. $graphLookup performs breadth-first search with iterative $lookups internally. In Cassandra: need to manually denormalize. Table: user_friends, user_likes. Query step-by-step with multiple coordinator requests. Graph databases beat others in deep, multi-hop relationship queries.

B+ Tree: height-balanced tree. All records in leaves. Leaves linked (sequential access). Order = p. Index node max p children, min ceil(p/2). Insert: find leaf, place entry. If overflow, split into two nodes, push separator key to parent. Root split increases tree height. Delete: find leaf, remove entry. Underflow: if node has less than minimum entries, try redistribution from adjacent sibling via parent. If redistribution impossible, merge nodes, delete parent separator. Tree shrinks if root loses all entries. Search: binary search within node, traverse downwards. Range query: locate first leaf, follow next pointers. I/O cost: height = ceil(log_ceil(p/2)(N)). For N=1M, p=100, height=3. So 3 I/Os for lookup. ISAM: static multilevel index. Data pages in sorted file. Index pages point to data pages. Overflow pages for inserts. Search: traverse index, then scan data page + overflow chain. Fast if no overflow. As table grows, performance deteriorates. Rebuild required periodically. Linear Hashing: dynamic hashing. Family of hash functions: hi(k) = k mod (2^i * N). Split pointer p tracks next bucket to split. Insert: hash using current level, if bucket >= p, hash using next level. If bucket full, add overflow. When load factor > threshold, split bucket p, redistribute, increment p. Search: 1-2 I/Os average depending on overflow. Good for growing table with point queries. Fill factor: fraction of index page used. High fill factor (e.g., 0.8) means pages mostly full, good for read performance (fewer pages to scan) but inserts may cause frequent splits. Low fill factor (e.g., 0.5) speeds inserts but wastes space. B+ Trees allow specifying fill factor to tune.

Bitmap indexes: vector of bits per distinct column value. For predicate 'color=red AND size=L', two bitmaps AND'ed quickly. Best suited for low cardinality (few distinct values) and read-intensive workloads. Updates are expensive (must modify multiple bitmaps). Can be compressed (Roaring bitmap, EWAH). R-Tree: balanced tree for spatial objects. Each node entry is (bounding box, pointer). Insertion chooses subtree requiring least area enlargement. Queries: containment, overlap, nearest neighbor using distance metrics. Used in PostGIS, Oracle Spatial. Inverted index: for keyword search. Lexicon (term dictionary) with pointer to postings list. Postings list: sorted doc IDs. Variant: contains positions for proximity search. Boolean expression: (t1 AND t2) = merge intersection of postings list. Data warehouse (star schema): Fact table 'Sales' (fact columns: amount, quantity; dimension keys: date_key, product_key, store_key). Index strategy: B+ tree on primary key (surrogate). Bitmap indexes on each dimension foreign key for fast star joins (Oracle star transformation converts bitmap OR operation on dimension filter to single fact access). Bitmap join index: create bitmap representing dimension value mapping to fact rows. Example: product.category='Electronics' bitmap applied directly to Fact rows, eliminating join. Covering index: composite index on frequently used columns plus INCLUDE. Example: ON Sales (date_key, product_key) INCLUDE (amount). Query: SELECT SUM(amount) FROM Sales WHERE date_key BETWEEN 20250101 AND 20250131 AND product_key = 500. Uses index-only scan. Materialized view: pre-computed aggregation. MV Sales_Summary AS SELECT date_key, product_key, SUM(amount) total FROM Sales GROUP BY date_key, product_key. Query optimizer rewrites to use MV when query matches.

Index-only scans: also called covering index scan. If all output columns are in index, and visibility map indicates all tuples on page are visible to all transactions, heap access skipped. In EXPLAIN, 'Index Only Scan' (PostgreSQL) or 'index only scan' in Oracle. Requires careful index design. GiST: Generalized Search Tree. Implements balance tree for complex data types. Used for: full-text search (tsvector, tsquery), geometric types (box, circle, point), range types, arrays. Index method implemented via 7 user-defined functions (consistent, union, compress, decompress, penalty, picksplit, same). GIN: Generalized Inverted Index. Used for: arrays, JSONB, tsvector (full text). Indexes composite items by extracting elements (e.g., words, keys) and indexing them separately. Search: each key maps to posting list; AND/OR of posting lists. For JSONB: default GIN operator class (jsonb_ops) indexes all keys, values, and array elements. jsonb_path_ops indexes only path/value combinations (more compact). Example: CREATE INDEX ON products USING GIN (specifications jsonb_path_ops); Query: SELECT name FROM products WHERE specifications @> '{"color":"red","size":"large"}'; EXPLAIN ANALYZE shows: Bitmap Index Scan -> Bitmap Heap Scan. Bitmap: collects TIDs from index for both path conditions, ANDs them. Heap scan: fetches pages. Seq scan: reads all rows, filters JSONB. Planner estimates cost: Seq Scan cost = seq_page_cost * N_pages + cpu_cost * N_tuples. Index scan: startup cost (index traversal) + random_page_cost * estimated matching pages. Explain output: (cost=0.00..125.00 rows=5 width=32) ... Actual: rows=5 loops=1. Shared buffers hit indicates cache usage. Bitmap scan chosen over index scan when multiple rows qualify, reducing random I/O by sorting TIDs per page.

Conflict Serializability definition: A schedule S is conflict serializable if there exists a serial schedule S' such that S can be transformed to S' by a series of swaps of non-conflicting adjacent operations. Precedence graph test: acyclic. View Serializability: less restrictive. Two schedules are view-equivalent if for each data item: (1) the first read is from the same source (initial or same transaction); (2) each read operation reads the value written by the same transaction; (3) the last writer is the same. View serializability allows blind writes that conflict serializability rejects. Example: let T1: W(A), T2: W(A), T3: R(A). Schedule: W1(A), W2(A), R3(A). Conflict graph: W1(A)->W2(A): T1->T2; W2(A)->R3(A): T2->T3. No cycle from T3 to others. So this IS conflict serializable (T1->T2->T3). Need non-conflict-serializable. Use blind write creating cycle. S: R1(A), W2(A), W1(B), W2(B), R3(B). Actually R1(A) then W2(A): T1->T2. W1(B) then W2(B): T1->T2 (same direction, no cycle). So conflict-serializable. Classic example: S: R1(A), W2(A), W2(B), W1(B). Conflict: R1(A)->W2(A) (T1->T2). W2(B)->W1(B) (T2->T1). Cycle! Not conflict-serializable. Check view: Serial T1,T2: R1(A) W1(B) W2(A) W2(B). Initial A: not read? In S, T1 reads A, then T2 writes A. In serial T1,T2: T1 reads initial A, then writes B, then T2 writes A, B. Final A=T2, B=T2. In S: T1 reads A (initial), T2 writes A, T2 writes B, T1 writes B (final B=T1). So final B different (T1 vs T2). View not equivalent to T1,T2. Try T2,T1: W2(A) W2(B) R1(A?) T1 hasn't read A in S? Wait S has R1(A) at start. In T2,T1 serial: W2(A) W2(B) R1(A) ... R1 reads A from T2, not initial. So initial read of A differs. So not view-equivalent to either. Textbooks have a specific example with three transactions for view but not conflict.

Thomas' Write Rule vs Basic TO vs Strict 2PL: Basic Timestamp Ordering (TO): each transaction assigned unique timestamp. Operations checked: Read(Q): if TS(T) < W_TS(Q), abort (reading stale). Else allowed, set R_TS(Q) = max(R_TS(Q), TS(T)). Write(Q): if TS(T) < R_TS(Q) or TS(T) < W_TS(Q), abort (write conflict). Else allowed, set W_TS(Q)=TS(T). Thomas' Write Rule: same as TO except Write(Q): if TS(T) < R_TS(Q), abort; if TS(T) < W_TS(Q), ignore the write (do nothing, no abort). Rationale: write is obsolete and can be safely discarded. Strict 2PL: lock-based. Obtain S-lock before read, X-lock before write. All X-locks held until commit/abort. S-locks can be released earlier (but Strict 2PL holds all until commit). Scenario: T1(TS=10), T2(TS=20). Sequence: T1 reads A (locked S, R_TS=10). T2 writes A (needs X-lock). Strict 2PL: T2 waits. TO: T2 allowed, sets W_TS=20. T1 then writes B: TO checks R_TS, W_TS of B (ok). But what if T1 writes A later? TS(10) < W_TS(20): TO aborts T1. Thomas' Write Rule: ignores T1's write, no abort. Starvation: in TO, restart with same timestamp causes cycle of aborts. Solution: restart with new (larger) timestamp. Strict 2PL: deadlock possible; resolution by wound-wait or wait-die. Cascading rollback: TO may require cascading rollback if a transaction reads from uncommitted transaction that later aborts. Strict 2PL avoids this because T2 cannot read uncommitted T1's writes (X-locks prevent read).

Complex query: SELECT p.pname, SUM(o.quantity*o.price) FROM products p, orders o, customers c WHERE p.pid = o.pid AND o.cid = c.cid AND c.city = 'Colombo' AND p.category = 'Electronics' AND o.order_date >= '2025-01-01' GROUP BY p.pname HAVING SUM(o.quantity*o.price) > 10000. Canonical tree: PROJECT(pname, sum) -> HAVING(>10000) -> GROUP BY(pname) -> SELECT(city='Colombo' AND category='Electronics' AND date>='2025-01-01' AND p.pid=o.pid AND o.cid=c.cid) -> CROSS(products, orders, customers). Heuristic: split SELECTs: σ(city='Colombo') -> customers; σ(category='Electronics') -> products; σ(date>='2025-01-01') -> orders. Convert CROSS+σ(equalities) to JOINs: customers ⋈ orders, then orders ⋈ products. Push projections: project needed attributes early. Order JOIN: smallest result first. Let's say city filter reduces customers to 100 rows; category reduces products to 200; date reduces orders to 10000. Join order: (customers ⋈ orders) ⋈ products. Optimized tree: π -> γ -> ⋈(pid) -> ( ⋈(cid) -> (σ(customers) π), (σ(orders) π) ), (σ(products) π). Materialization: intermediate joins saved to disk if large. Pipelining: one join's output streams directly to next. Example: Nested loop join: left side materialized (outer), right pipelined (inner). Cost: 100 (customers) + 100*10000 (orders) = 1,000,100 for first join. Result size? Assuming each customer has 10 orders = 1000 rows. Second join: 1000*200 = 200,000. Total ~1.2M block accesses. With indexes on keys: much lower.

Cost-based optimizer: estimates cost of plans. Uses statistics collected by ANALYZE command. Example statistics: reltuples (row count), relpages (page count). Per column: null_frac, avg_width, n_distinct, most_common_vals/freqs (MCV), histogram_bounds. Selectivity estimation: equality col=val: if val in MCV, selectivity=MCV_freq; else selectivity = (1 - sum(MCV_freqs)) / (n_distinct - MCV_len). Range col>val: use histogram to find fraction of values > val. Heuristic optimizer: rules-based, no stats. Operation ordering rules. Modern optimizers use heuristics for rewriting before cost estimation. Correlated subquery: inner references outer. Nested loops pattern. Decorrelation: rewriting to join/apply. (1) Scalar subquery: SELECT e.*, (SELECT d.name FROM dept d WHERE d.id = e.dept_id) FROM emp e. Rewrite: SELECT e.*, d.name FROM emp e LEFT JOIN dept d ON d.id = e.dept_id. (2) EXISTS: SELECT * FROM emp e WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM sales s WHERE s.emp_id = e.id). Rewrite: SELECT DISTINCT e.* FROM emp e JOIN sales s ON e.id = s.emp_id (or semi-join). Optimizer error: outliers in data. Column 'income' has 99% values under 100K, 1% over 1M. Histogram bucket for high income is large range avg 1M but only few values. Opt estimates high selectivity, chooses parallel scan, but only 10 rows, index would be faster. Or outdated stats cause poor plan selection.

CAP Theorem: proof by Gilbert & Lynch. In distributed systems, only 2 of consistency, availability, partition tolerance possible. Partition tolerance necessary (network failures). CP systems: during partition, sacrifice availability to maintain consistency. AP systems: sacrifice consistency (return possibly stale data) to remain available. Cassandra: AP. Eventual consistency. Configurable via consistency level (ONE, QUORUM, ALL). Write CL=QUORUM + Read CL=QUORUM with RF=3 gives overlap -> strong consistency (effectively CP mode). MongoDB replica set: CP. Primary holds writes. If primary partitioned, election held, majority elects new primary. No writes until new primary, sacrificing availability. Spanner: CP. Google's globally distributed DB uses TrueTime (atomic clocks) to ensure external consistency (strongest level). Requires quorum for writes. DynamoDB: AP default. Client can request strongly consistent read (uses quorum, may be unavailable during partition). Tunable consistency: clients can trade off for each operation. In Cassandra, setting lower consistency levels tolerates more failures but gives eventual consistency. Setting higher requires more replicas up, giving strong consistency.

Distributed database for 500M social: Data partitioned across 10,000+ shards by user_id (hash partitioning). Each shard replicated 3× within region (Raft group) and asynchronous across regions. Posts: stored in shard by author_id with post_id sorting. Timeline: list of post IDs pre-computed (fanout on write) into each follower's timeline shard. Consistency: strong for billing/payments - use separate accounting service with ACID (sharded by account_id, 2PC across shards). Weak for social feed: CRDTs. Unread counts: PN-Counter. Post likes: G-Counter. Comments: Add to list with unique ID (Grow-Only Set). Conflict resolution: automatic via CRDT merge properties. CRDTs are monotonic and converge. Network partition: each datacenter runs independently. For partition healing, nodes exchange Merkle trees. Differing keys identified, values merged using CRDT logic. For non-CRDT data, use last-writer-wins with hybrid logical clocks (HLC). HLC combines physical time with logical counter: (wall_clock_time, logical). Provides global ordering (approximately). HLC ensures causality is respected, while LWW resolves conflicts deterministically.

Document store: MongoDB stores BSON documents. Rich queries, indexing, aggregation. Good: flexible schema, evolving data. Bad: complex joins slow, deep nesting limited. Wide-column store: Cassandra organizes data by partition key and clustering columns. Optimized for heavy writes, append-only. Query design upfront required. Good: time-series, logging, high-velocity data. Bad: no JOINs, limited ad-hoc querying. Graph DB: Neo4j uses native graph storage. Nodes and edges stored as objects. Relationship traversal via direct pointers is O(1). Cypher language is expressive. Social network query 'friends of friends who liked same post': Cypher: MATCH (me:User {id:'me'})-[:FRIEND]->(f1)-[:FRIEND]->(f2), (me)-[:LIKED]->(:Post {id:'p1'})<-[:LIKED]-(f2) RETURN f2. Execution engine traverses from 'me', FRIEND edges to f1 (1st hop), then FRIEND edges to f2 (2nd hop). For each f2, checks if LIKED relationship to post exists (O(1) per f2, as node's relationships are directly accessible). This is highly efficient even for millions of users. In MongoDB: $graphLookup does similar expansion but via recursive $lookup (index lookups per hop). In Cassandra: data duplicated into tables; searching across relationships requires multiple queries and application-side processing. Graph database is the most natural and performant for this type of highly-connected data query.

B+ Tree: balanced tree index structure. Root, internal nodes (keys, child ptrs), leaf nodes (keys+data ptrs, next ptr). Order m: internal max m children; leaf max m-1 key-value pairs. Insert: Locate leaf. Insert. If overflow, split into two, promote separator to parent. Deletion: Remove from leaf. Underflow (< ceil(m/2) entries for internal or leaves). Try rebalancing (borrow from sibling). Else merge. Adjust parent. Search: O(log n) I/O. Range scan: leaf chain traversal. ISAM: Indexed Sequential Access Method. Static multilevel index. Created initially from sorted data. Data pages sequential. Index pages point to data page ranges. Overflow pages chained for inserts. Range scan: traverse leaf pages and overflow chains. Degrades with updates; periodic reorganization needed. Linear Hashing: dynamic hashing. Hash functions h_level(k) = k mod (N * 2^level). Split pointer. Insert: compute hash; if bucket >= split ptr use current level else next. If bucket full, chain overflow. Check load factor; split bucket at split ptr, move split ptr. Splits spread evenly. Search: direct bucket access with 0-1 overflow page access (average). Fill factor impacts performance. B+Tree fill factor: target page occupancy after split. Postgres default 90% for indexes. Higher coalesces space, reduces splits, but leaves less room leading to future splits. Good for read-mostly. Lower (70%) speeds inserts. Linear hashing load factor = N / (buckets * capacity). Standard 0.7-0.8. More splits at low load factor. ISAM: initial fill 100% but overflow chains fill subsequent space.

Bitmap index: per value bit vector. Good for low-cardinality columns (e.g., marital_status: single, married, divorced). Bitwise AND/OR/NOT execute quickly on hardware. Used in Oracle, PostgreSQL (contrib). Bitmap join index: maps dimension table column values to fact table rows. Created by CREATE BITMAP INDEX ... ON fact(dim.column) FROM fact, dim WHERE ...; Oracle implementation. In data warehousing, star transformation: query filters on dimension tables, generates bitmap from dimension, OR-merges if multiple values, ANDs across dimensions, resulting bitmap accesses fact rows directly. Covering index: includes all columns needed by query. In SQL Server: CREATE NONCLUSTERED INDEX idx ON table(col1) INCLUDE (col2, col3). Allows index-only scan. Materialized view: pre-computed result. CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW mv_sales_summary BUILD IMMEDIATE REFRESH FAST ON COMMIT AS SELECT ... FROM fact JOIN dim ... GROUP BY ... Query rewrite: optimizer automatically redirects query to MV if semantically equivalent and cost lower. Example MV: Sales SUM by day and product. Query for monthly sales by product: aggregates over daily MV rather than high-volume fact table. R-Tree: spatial index. Key: Minimum Bounding Rectangle (MBR). Used for geographic data, CAD. Supports operations: ST_Contains, ST_Intersects, ST_Distance. Inverted index: for unstructured text. Term -> posting list. Boolean query: intersect posting lists for AND. Proximity query: positional index needed.

Index-only scan: query executor retrieves all required data from index, no heap fetch. Benefits: reduces I/O, avoids random access to heap. Requirements: index contains all SELECT list and WHERE clause column values. In PostgreSQL, index must include all columns (INCLUDE clause for non-key columns). Also, heap page must be visible to all transactions (checked via visibility map). If not, must visit heap to confirm tuple visibility. GiST index: Generalized Search Tree. Extensible indexing framework. Balanced tree. Used for: geometric types (point, box, polygon), network address (inet, cidr), full text, range types. GiST supports many operators: <<, &<, &>, >>, <<|, @>, <@, ~=. GIN index: Generalized Inverted Index. Used where items to be indexed are composite values (arrays, JSON, tsvector). For JSONB: default jsonb_ops indexes all keys, values, array elements -> large. jsonb_path_ops indexes only full path/value combinations -> compact, efficient for @> operator. CREATE INDEX idx1 ON t USING GIN (j jsonb_path_ops); Query: SELECT * FROM t WHERE j @> '{"a":1, "b":2}'; This finds rows where JSONB contains both a=1 and b=2. Explain output: Bitmap Index Scan on idx1 (cost=0.00..12.00 rows=10 width=...). Then Bitmap Heap Scan on t. The index finds TIDs for the two conditions, ANDs them (if both required), returns bitmap. Bitmap Heap Scan reads heap pages in physical order, minimizing random I/O. Seq Scan would read all rows and evaluate JSONB condition. Index Scan: (for btree) Index Cond: (column = value). EXPLAIN shows 'Index Scan using idx on table'. This is direct index access with heap fetch. Selection between bitmap and index scan depends on correlation, number of rows returned. Planner uses cost estimates to decide.

Conflict Serializability: Two operations conflict if they are on same data item and at least one is write. A schedule S is conflict equivalent to S' if S can be transformed to S' by swapping non-conflicting operations. Conflict serializable if conflict equivalent to some serial schedule. Test: Build precedence graph (nodes=transactions, edge Ti->Tj if operation in Ti conflicts with later operation in Tj). Schedule is conflict serializable iff graph is acyclic. View Serializability: S is view equivalent to S' if: 1) Initial read of each item is from same source (initial DB or same transaction). 2) For each read, the transaction that wrote the value read is the same. 3) Final writer of each item is same transaction. Example of view-serializable but not conflict: S: W1(X), W2(X), W2(Y), R3(X). We need R3 to read from W2. Add W1's read... Known example: S: R1(A), W2(A), W1(B), W2(B), R3(A). Not conflict-serializable because T1->T2 (on A) and T2->T1 (on B) cycle. View check: Is it view equivalent to T1,T2,T3? Let's formally define: I'll use standard example from textbook with blind writes creating the difference.

Thomas' Write Rule (TWR): Uses timestamps. Data item Q has R_TS (max timestamp of transactions that read Q) and W_TS (max timestamp that wrote Q). Rules: Read(Q) by Ti: if TS(Ti) < W_TS(Q), abort (reading overwritten value). Else allow, set R_TS(Q) = max(R_TS(Q), TS(Ti)). Write(Q) by Ti: if TS(Ti) < R_TS(Q), abort (item already read by younger transaction). else if TS(Ti) < W_TS(Q), ignore Write (value already overwritten by younger transaction). else process Write, set W_TS(Q)=TS(Ti). Basic TO: aborts instead of ignoring on second condition. Strict 2PL: uses locks. Growing phase: acquire locks. Shrinking phase: release locks (strict: all X locks held till commit). Scenario analysis on X, Y: T1 (old) and T2 (young). T1 reads X (S-lock, R_OK). T1 writes Y (X-lock, W_OK). T2 reads Y (needs S-lock, waits for T1 X-lock release -> strict 2PL waits). T2 writes X (needs X-lock, same). In TO: T2 allowed if no conflicting timestamps, sets timestamps. Then T1's later operations might abort. Thomas: ignores obsolete writes. Starvation: TO can starve if transaction repeatedly aborted (must use fair restarts with new timestamps). Strict 2PL: starvation due to deadlock aborts but priority mechanisms exist. Cascading Rollback: prevented by strict 2PL (no dirty reads). Possible in TO (if reading uncommitted data).

Query: SELECT e.name, d.name FROM employee e, department d, project p, works_on w WHERE e.id = w.emp_id AND p.id = w.proj_id AND e.dept_id = d.id AND p.budget > 1000000 AND e.salary > 80000 GROUP BY e.name, d.name. Canonical tree: π(name, name) -> γ(e.name, d.name) -> σ(budget>1M AND salary>80K AND e.id=w.emp_id AND p.id=w.proj_id AND e.dept_id=d.id) -> ×(e, d, p, w). Heuristic: split σ, push σ(salary>80K) to e, σ(budget>1M) to p. Replace × + equi-conditions with ⋈. Order: smallest after push: e (filtered), p (filtered), d, w. Join graph: e-dept(d), e-works(w)-proj(p). Join order: (e ⋈ w) ⋈ p ⋈ d. Push projection early. Materialized vs Pipelined evaluation: materialized stores intermediate join results (e ⋈ w) to disk; pipelined passes tuples directly. Dependent on join method. Hash join: builds hash table (materialized build input), probes with other (streamed). Sort-merge: both inputs must be sorted (materialized if not pre-sorted). Nested loop: outer is materialized/pipelined? Outer scanned once (materialized or pipelined based on buffer). Pipelining reduces I/O cost but requires more memory coordination.

Cost-based optimization (CBO) relies on statistics gathered from data. Statistics: table size (number of pages, number of tuples), column statistics (number of distinct values, null fraction, average width, histograms). Cost model: estimates I/O (page fetches) and CPU (processing rows). Total cost = (seq_page_cost * pages_seq) + (random_page_cost * pages_random) + (cpu_tuple_cost * rows). Plan space searched via dynamic programming (System R algorithm). Heuristic rules: don't require statistics; e.g., always push selection before join, replace cross-products with joins. Used in early stages (query rewrite) or for simple optimizers. Correlated subqueries: e.g., SELECT * FROM e WHERE salary > (SELECT AVG(salary) FROM e e2 WHERE e2.dept_id = e.dept_id). For each outer row, subquery runs -> O(N^2). Decorrelation: rewrite to JOIN with derived table: SELECT e.* FROM e JOIN (SELECT dept_id, AVG(salary) avg_s FROM e GROUP BY dept_id) d ON e.dept_id = d.dept_id WHERE e.salary > d.avg_s. Now O(N log N). Optimizer may fail: if statistics outdated. Example: auto-ANALYZE threshold not reached, table has 10x more rows. Optimizer uses old row count 100K while actual 1M. Chooses index scan expecting 10 rows, but actual 5000 rows, leading to bad performance compared to sequential scan. Or mis-estimates join cardinality due to assumption of independence between predicates.

CAP Theorem: A distributed system cannot simultaneously provide Consistency (all nodes see same data at same time), Availability (every request gets a non-error response), and Partition Tolerance (system operates despite network partition). Since partitions occur, only CP or AP possible. Cassandra (AP by default): eventual consistency. Replicas accept writes even during partition. Conflict resolution via Last Write Wins (LWW) or CRDTs. Consistency levels: ONE, TWO, THREE, QUORUM, LOCAL_QUORUM, ALL. QUORUM provides strong consistency if R+W > N. MongoDB replica set (CP): uses single primary for writes. If primary fails, automatic election of new primary; during election (typically few seconds), no writes accepted. Secondary can serve stale reads. Spanner (CP): uses TrueTime for global consistency. Transactions use two-phase commit and Paxos. Provides external consistency (strictest isolation). DynamoDB (AP default): synchronous replication, eventual consistent reads, optional strongly consistent reads via quorum. Tunable consistency: application can specify consistency level per operation. In Cassandra, write CL=ONE gives high availability but weak consistency. Write CL=ALL gives strong consistency but unavailable if any node down. Application can trade-off based on business needs.

System design for 500M users: Use microservice architecture with polyglot persistence. User service: graph DB for social graph. Post service: wide-column store. Partitioning: hash by user_id for user data, by post_id for post media. Replication factor 3 within each regional cluster. Global distribution: 5 geo-regions. Consistency: financial transactions: ACID using Spanner or CockroachDB. For social interactions (likes, shares): CRDT-based. OR-Set for shared_posts (add post_id with unique tag, remove by tag). G-Counter for likes. LWW-Element-Set for followers. Vector clocks capture causality. Conflict detection: compare vector clocks. If VCa < VCb (VCa dominates), then VCa's version is newer. If concurrent, merge using CRDT rules. Network partition: use active-active multi-master replication across regions. Accept writes locally. Sync with Merkle trees upon heal. Read-repair: during read, check multiple replicas, resolve and write back consistent value. For strict financial data: require consensus across regions (Paxos/Raft). This sacrifices availability during partition (CP) but ensures no double-charge. Split brain prevention: use quorum-based leader election, fence tokens to prevent old leader from acting.

Document model (MongoDB): JSON/BSON docs in collections. Rich queries, aggregation framework, secondary indexes. Embedded documents for one-to-one/one-to-few relationships. References for one-to-many. Good for content management, user profiles, IoT data. Wide-column (Cassandra): data organized as rows with partition key and clustering columns. Efficient range queries within partition. Write-optimized storage (LSM Tree). No joins; should denormalize. Good for time-series logs, monitoring data, recommendation engine data (e.g., user recent actions). Graph model (Neo4j): nodes, edges with types, properties. Native graph storage with pointers for relationships. Index-free adjacency: each node stores direct references to its relationships, allowing O(1) traversal per hop. Best for strongly connected data and queries that traverse multiple hops. For social network 'friends of friends who liked same post': In Neo4j: MATCH (u:User)-[:FRIEND*2]-(fof:User)-[:LIKED]->(p:Post), (u)-[:LIKED]->(p) WHERE u.id = 'x' RETURN fof. Database engine performs graph traversal: start node 'x', expand outgoing FRIEND edges (1st level), for each friend, expand their FRIEND edges (2nd level), for each candidate, check LIKED edge to post. Index-free adjacency means expanding a node's relationships is pointer-following, extremely fast. In MongoDB: $graphLookup does similar but via $lookup per level, each requiring index scans. For deep traversals, this overhead multiplies significantly, making graph DB much faster.

B+ Tree: Balanced multi-way tree where all leaves are at same level and linked sequentially. Internal nodes: n keys and n+1 pointers. Leaf nodes: key-data pointer pairs. Order p: internal node up to p pointers. Insert: find leaf, insert entry. If leaf has > p entries (overflow), split leaf, create new leaf with ceil(p/2) entries, promote separator to parent. If parent overflows, split and promote upwards. Deletion: find leaf, delete entry. If leaf underflows (entries < ceil(p/2)), attempt to borrow from sibling. If borrow fails, merge with sibling, delete parent separator; propagate. Search: O(log_p N) I/Os. ISAM: static structure built on sorted data file. Index levels point to cylinder/page ranges. Inserts go to overflow area chained to data page. Good for static files; degrades with inserts/updates. Reorganization (rebuild) needed. Linear Hashing: dynamic hash structure, no directory. Hash function family: hi(k) = k mod (M * 2^i). Split pointer sp tracks bucket to split. Insert: if bucket >= sp, use h_level; else use h_level+1. Attempt insert, if overflow, add overflow bucket. Periodically split bucket sp, increment sp, and rehash entries in sp-1. Search: direct bucket via hash. Overflow chains scanned sequentially. Average search: ~1.05 I/Os. Range queries: B+ Trees excel (leaf linked list). Linear Hashing not for range queries. ISAM supports range but performance drops with updates. Fill factor: controls page density. B+Tree FILLFACTOR (Postgres) specifies percentage fill for leaf pages during rebuild; default 90%. Low fill = room for inserts, less splitting; high fill = compact, faster reads.

Bitmap index: array of bits for each key value in column. Efficient for low cardinality columns: e.g., region (North, South, East, West). For query with region='North' AND year=2025, bitwise AND of two bitmaps selects rows. Compressed bitmaps (Roaring) handle sparse bitmaps. R-Tree: hierarchical data structure for spatial objects. Each node entry is (minimum bounding rectangle, child ptr). Queries: intersection, containment, distance. Used in GIS. Inverted index: for full-text. Term dictionary (B-tree/hash) maps term to posting list (sorted doc IDs). Boolean search: for AND, intersect two posting lists (O(|p1|+|p2|)). For data warehouse star schema: Fact table (transaction_id, date_id, product_id, store_id, amount). Indexing: B-tree on date_id for range queries. Bitmap index on product_id, store_id for low cardinality filtering. Bitmap join index: CREATE BITMAP INDEX fact_prod_cat ON fact(product.category) FROM fact, product WHERE fact.product_id = product.id. Stores product.category bitmap directly into fact. For query 'sum of sales for electronics in Q1': bitmap join index for category='Electronics' AND-ed with date range bitmap, produces fact rows to aggregate. Covering index: include frequently queried columns. CREATE INDEX idx_cov ON fact(product_id, store_id) INCLUDE (amount). Queries for amount by product+store use only index. Materialized view: CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW mv_quarter_sales BUILD IMMEDIATE REFRESH COMPLETE AS SELECT product_id, store_id, quarter, sum(amount) total FROM fact JOIN date_dim ... GROUP BY product_id, store_id, quarter. Subsequent aggregate queries reuse MV.

Index-only scans (covering index scans): Index contains all columns needed for query; heap access is avoided. PostgreSQL: 'Index Only Scan' in EXPLAIN. Condition: all queried columns in index + all heap pages fully visible (visibility map). Big performance gain for I/O bound OLAP queries. GiST index: Generalized Search Tree. Supports complex data types. Balanced tree of node entries, each entry is a 'predicate' that holds for all entries below. Queries traverse nodes where predicate is consistent with query. Used for: geometry (PostGIS), full text (tsvector), array, range types. Example: CREATE INDEX ON rides USING GiST (trip box_ops); for spatial bounding box queries. GIN index: Generalized Inverted Index. For values that are composite (multiple elements). Contains: B-tree over entry keys + posting lists/Trees. Used for arrays (int[], text[]), JSON, full text (tsvector). JSONB GIN: jsonb_ops indexes each key, value, array element. Creates large index. jsonb_path_ops indexes only entire path/value hash, compact. CREATE INDEX ON products USING GIN (specs jsonb_path_ops); SELECT name FROM products WHERE specs @> '{"ram":"16GB","cpu":"i7"}'::jsonb; EXPLAIN ANALYZE: Bitmap Index Scan on idx -> Bitmap Heap Scan. The index lookup finds TIDs for each predicate path, combines via AND. Bitmap Heap Scan then fetches pages in order. Seq Scan for comparison shows much higher cost (seq scan of all product pages). Difference between sequential, bitmap index, and index scan: Seq scan reads all blocks sequentially, efficient if high selectivity. Index scan directly fetches tuple by TID, good for very few tuples. Bitmap combines TIDs from index, sorts by block, fetches each block once.

Conflict serializability: based on the notion of swapping adjacent non-conflicting operations to achieve a serial schedule. Conflict occurs when operations are from different transactions, same data item, at least one write. Precedence graph: Ti -> Tj if conflicting ops and Ti's op precedes Tj's. Cycle => not conflict serializable. View serializability: less strict, considers the reads-from relationship and final writes. Two schedules are view-equivalent if: 1) Same initial reads (transactions reading before any write). 2) Same read-from mapping (every read reads value from same write). 3) Same final writes (last writer of each item). Blind writes (writes without reading) can cause conflict cycles but still be view-serializable. Example (from Korth): T1: W(A); T2: W(A); T3: R(A). Schedule: W1(A), W2(A), R3(A). Conflict graph: T1->T2 (W-W), T2->T3 (W-R), T1->T3 (W-R). No cycle -> conflict serializable. Need blind writes that create conflict cycle but view-equivalent. Example: T1: R(A), W(B); T2: W(A), R(B). Schedule S: R1(A), W2(A), W1(B), R2(B). Conflict: R1(A)-W2(A): T1->T2. W1(B)-R2(B): T1->T2 (same direction). No cycle -> conflict serializable. Not the example. The standard example uses three transactions: T1: W(A); T2: W(A), W(B); T3: R(B). S: W1(A), W2(A), W2(B), R3(B). Conflict: T1->T2 (W-W A). T2->T3 (W-R B). No cycle. Its known example of view-serializable but not conflict: S: R1(A), W2(A), W1(B), W2(B), R3(B). Let's check conflict: R1(A)->W2(A): T1->T2. W1(B)->W2(B): T1->T2? Wait, W1(B) then W2(B): W-W conflict T1->T2. Still single direction. Need opposite directions: S: R1(A), W2(A), W2(B), W1(B). Conflict: R1(A)->W2(A): T1->T2; W2(B)->W1(B): T2->T1. Cycle! Not conflict. Is it view-serializable? Check equivalence to T1,T2? Serial T1,T2: R1(A) W1(B) W2(A) W2(B). Final: A=T2, B=T2. In S: final A=T2, B=T1. Different. So not view-equivalent to T1,T2. Try T2,T1: W2(A) W2(B) R1(A) W1(B). Final: A=T1? Actually A written by T2 then T1? Wait, final W on A is T2 (then T1 reads, no write). But W1(B) then W2(B) in S has final B=T1. In serial: W2(B) W1(B) final B=T1. A: T2 writes A, T1 reads. Final A=T2. Matches S. So view-equivalent to T2,T1, but not conflict-serializable (cycle). This illustrates the concept.

Thomas' Write Rule (TWR) - modification of Timestamp Ordering protocol: When transaction Ti wants to write item Q, check: if TS(Ti) < R_TS(Q): abort (item already read by younger transaction). else if TS(Ti) < W_TS(Q): ignore write operation (obsolete write, already overwritten). else execute write, update W_TS(Q) = TS(Ti). Basic Timestamp Ordering (TO): same but aborts instead of ignoring in the second condition. Strict 2PL: Locks prevent conflicting accesses. Before read, acquire S-lock. Before write, acquire X-lock. Strict: all locks held until commit/abort (prevents cascading aborts). Scenario: Two transactions T1 (older, TS=10), T2 (younger, TS=20). Data items X, Y. Operations: T1: R(X), W(Y); T2: R(Y), W(X). Basic TO execution: T1 reads X (R_TS(X)=10). T2 reads Y (R_TS(Y)=20). T1 writes Y: TS(10) < R_TS(Y)=20 => abort T1. T2 writes X: TS(20) >= R_TS(X)=10, ok. Result: T1 aborted. Thomas' Write Rule: T1 write Y: TS(10) < W_TS(Y) currently 0, so allowed? Actually T2 hasn't written Y, only read. W_TS(Y) is 0. So TS(10) >= 0, allowed. T1 writes Y, sets W_TS(Y)=10. T2 then reads Y: allowed, R_TS becomes max(20,10)=20. T2 writes X: allowed. T1 commits (no further conflicts). But what if T2 wrote Y before T1? T2 writes Y (W_TS=20). T1 tries to write Y: TS(10) < W_TS(20) -> Thomas' Rule: ignore. Strict 2PL: T1 S-locks X, reads X. T1 X-locks Y, writes Y. T2 tries S-lock Y: waits until T1 commits. T2 tries X-lock X: waits. No concurrency, serial execution. Starvation/Deadlock: TO aborts can starve if same transaction repeatedly aborts. Strict 2PL may have deadlock. Cascading rollback: TO may see dirty reads if Write allows read before commit (not strict). Strict 2PL avoids by holding X locks.

Query: Retrieve total sales by product category for each month of 2025. Tables: Products(P), Sales(S), Time(T). SQL: SELECT P.category, T.month, SUM(S.amount) FROM Sales S, Products P, Time T WHERE S.product_id = P.id AND S.time_id = T.id AND T.year = 2025 GROUP BY P.category, T.month ORDER BY T.month, P.category. Canonical Tree: π(category, month, total) -> γ(category, month, SUM(amount)) -> σ(year=2025 AND S.product_id=P.id AND S.time_id=T.id) -> ×(S, P, T). Heuristic Optimization: split σ: σ(year=2025) pushed to T; σ(S.product_id=P.id) and σ(S.time_id=T.id) replaced by ⋈. Push projections: from P (id, category), T (id, month), S (product_id, time_id, amount). Optimized tree: π -> γ -> ⋈(S.product_id=P.id) -> ( ⋈(S.time_id=T.id) -> (π(S)), (σ+π(T)) ), (π(P)). Cost: size estimates: T filtered: 365 rows (1 year) -> ~1 page. Product: 1000 pages? Sales: 5M rows (5000 pages). Join order: (T ⋈ S) ⋈ P. First join: S (5000) with T (1 page). Nested loop: T outer (1), S inner (5000) -> 5000. Then join with P (1000) -> 5000*1000 = 5M. Hash join: (S ⋈ T): build hash on T (tiny), probe S (5000) -> 5000. Then hash join with P? Better: build hash on P (1000), probe with intermediate (~5000* selectivity). Pipelined Hash join: Build phase for P, then stream S⋈T output and probe. No materialization needed if hash table fits memory. If intermediate large, spill to disk.

Cost-based optimization: uses statistical metadata to estimate cost. Statistics collected via ANALYZE: table size (rows, blocks), per-column: null_frac, n_distinct, most_common_vals + frequencies, histogram_bounds, avg_width, correlation. Cost = (sequential_page_cost * pages_fetched_sequentially) + (random_page_cost * pages_fetched_randomly) + (cpu_cost * rows_processed). PostgreSQL default: seq_page_cost=1, random_page_cost=4. Path with minimal total cost chosen. Heuristic: applies algebra transformation rules. Examples: 'push down selection', 'replace cross join with inner join', 'eliminate useless projection'. Sometimes rules are incomplete or suboptimal without costing. Correlated subqueries: run once per outer row, causing O(N*M) complexity. Decorrelation transforms to join. Example: SELECT * FROM emp e WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM sales s WHERE s.emp_id = e.emp_id AND s.amount > 5000). Decorrelated: SELECT e.* FROM emp e JOIN sales s ON e.emp_id = s.emp_id WHERE s.amount > 5000 GROUP BY e.emp_id or use semi-join. User-defined functions (UDF) in WHERE clause cause optimizer issues: cost of UDF unknown, estimated as small constant, but expensive function leads to wrong plan selection. Outdated statistics after bulk load -> auto-vacuum hasn't updated -> planner thinks table empty -> uses index scan inappropriate.

CAP theorem: from Eric Brewer, formalized by Gilbert & Lynch. In distributed data stores, only two of Consistency, Availability, Partition Tolerance possible. Partition-tolerance: system works despite network failures (message loss). Since partitions happen, choice is CP or AP. Cassandra: AP by default. Eventual consistency. Writes to coordinator node, replicates to replicas asynchronously or with consistency level. Consistency levels: ANY (write to any replica, including hinted handoff), ONE, QUORUM (majority), ALL. Read repair ensures consistency eventually. MongoDB replica set: CP. All writes go through primary. Replication to secondaries is async. If primary fails, new primary elected; no writes possible during election (few seconds). Reads can be directed to secondary but may be stale. Spanner: CP. Global distributed database with strong external consistency. Uses TrueTime (GPS + atomic clocks) for globally ordered transactions. Writes use Paxos over replicas. Available as long as quorum reachable. DynamoDB: AP default. Eventual consistent reads (default). Strongly consistent read option uses quorum, costs more, may be unavailable during partition. Tunable consistency: in Cassandra, client can set consistency per statement. This allows tuning trade-off. Example: Write CL=LOCAL_QUORUM, Read CL=LOCAL_QUORUM for strong consistency within datacenter. Write CL=ONE for high availability (risk of stale reads).

Architecture: Global social platform with 500M users. Sharding: Consistent hashing ring with virtual nodes across geographically distributed nodes. Master-master replication between DCs for low-latency local writes. Partition key: user_id for user-centric data (profile, settings, follower list). Post_id for post content. Consistency: Financial transactions (ads, microtransactions) handled by separate strongly consistent service using ACID (might use Spanner, CockroachDB, or custom 2PC). Social updates (posts, likes) use CRDTs with causal consistency. CRDT types: G-Counter for likes/shares (merge: max). OR-Set for comments (add element with unique tag; remove by marking tag as removed). LWW-Element-Set for follower list. Causal consistency: reads return causally latest version; concurrent versions returned, application merges (or automatic CRDT). Use vector clocks for causality tracking. Conflict resolution: CRDTs provide automatic merge. For non-CRDT data, use LWW with conflict detection via vector clocks. Network partition: Multi-master allows acceptance of writes in all DCs during partition. On reconnect, Merkle tree exchange identifies divergent replicas. CRDTs merged, LWW conflicts resolved. Financial service: if partitioned, quorum unreachable, reject write (CP mode). Use fencing tokens to prevent split-brain in financial service.

Document DB (MongoDB): Data as BSON docs. Embed related data to avoid joins. Good for: User profiles (single document per user with embedded addresses, preferences). Wide-column (Cassandra): Data partitioned by partition key, sorted by clustering columns. Write optimized (append-only LSM tree). Good for: Event/time-series data, e.g., user clickstream, sensor data. Query design must match partition key. Graph DB (Neo4j): Native graph model. Nodes and relationships stored with direct pointers. Traversal follows pointers in O(1) per relationship. Excellent for: social network analysis, recommendation engines, fraud detection. For social network query 'friends of friends who liked same post': Neo4j: MATCH (a:User {id:'me'})-[:FRIEND*2]-(fof), (a)-[:LIKED]->(p:Post)<-[:LIKED]-(fof) RETURN fof. With index-free adjacency, expanding relationships is directly accessing the adjacency list stored in the node record. 1st hop: traverse friend edges from 'me'. 2nd hop: from each friend, traverse their friend edges. Check LIKED edge to post. Minimal pointer chasing, highly efficient. MongoDB: uses $graphLookup for multi-hop traversal. Internally conducts iterative $lookup+$unwind operations. For 2-hop, this is 2 joins, each requiring index lookups per parent row. Overhead far higher than pointer chasing. Cassandra: requires modeling data into tables specifically for this query pattern; typically involves denormalization and multiple queries, complex and slower for ad-hoc deep traversals. Graph DBs fundamentally optimized for deep relationships.

B+ Tree index: multi-level balanced tree. Search, insertion, deletion O(log_p N). Order p: internal node has p-1 keys, p pointers. Leaf: p-1 key-value pairs. Insertion: Locate leaf, insert. If overflow, split: left ceil(p/2)-1, right floor(p/2). Promote separator to parent. If parent overflows, recursive split upward. Deletion: Locate leaf, remove. If underflow (< ceil(p/2)-1), borrow from sibling (redistribute through parent). If borrow not possible, merge with sibling, delete parent key. Recursive. Range query: traverse leaf linked list. ISAM: Index Sequential Access Method. Static structure: data sorted in sequential pages; index pages point to cylinder overflow areas. Insertions go to overflow pages chained to data page. As overflow chains grow, performance deteriorates. Rebuild needed. Good for static master data. Linear Hashing: dynamic hashing. Hash function hi(k) = k mod (M * 2^i). Split pointer sp. Insert: hash using hl, if address >= sp use hl+1. Insert to bucket; if overflow, add overflow bucket. Split: when avgLoad > threshold, split bucket sp, rehash entries in sp using hl+1, increment sp. Search: 1 I/O ideally, plus overflow chain traversal. No range support. Comparison: B+ Tree best for range queries and dynamic data with good read/write balance. ISAM best for read-only historical data. Linear Hashing best for point queries on growing key sets. Fill factor: B+Tree fill factor (FILLFACTOR) controls how full leaf pages are created during index rebuild or split. Default 90% (PostgreSQL). High fill = more keys per node, fewer levels, good for reads. Low fill = headroom for inserts, reduces splits, good for write-heavy. ISAM: initial 100% fill. Linear hashing: load factor before split (typical 0.75).

Bitmap indexes: each distinct value has a bitmap (length = #rows). Bit 1 means row has that value. Boolean operations combine bitmaps (AND, OR, NOT). Best for low-cardinality, boolean, and read mostly. Can be compressed (Roaring bitmaps). Widely used in data warehouses (Oracle, PostgreSQL). R-Tree: spatial index. Organizes objects by their bounding rectangles. Hierarchical MBRs. Good for geometric range queries (find points in bounding box) and nearest-neighbor queries. Used in PostGIS, Oracle Spatial. Inverted index: full-text search. Lexicon (terms) + posting lists (document IDs). Supports phrase search via positional index. Good for text search engines. Data warehouse indexing: Star schema: Fact(FactID, DateKey, ProductKey, StoreKey, Amount). Strategy: 1) Bitmap index on DateKey, ProductKey, StoreKey. If dimension attributes need filtering, use bitmap join index (Oracle): CREATE BITMAP INDEX fact_cust_city ON fact(customer_dim.city) FROM fact, customer_dim WHERE fact.cust_key = customer_dim.cust_key. This pre-joins and creates bitmap mapping dimension values to fact rows. 2) Materialized view: CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW store_product_month_mv AS SELECT store_key, product_key, month, SUM(amount) total FROM fact, date_dim WHERE fact.date_key = date_dim.date_key GROUP BY store_key, product_key, month. MV with query rewrite offloads aggregation queries. 3) Covering index on fact: create index on frequently combined keys with INCLUDE for measures. Supports index-only scans for specific queries.

Index-only scan: Query reads data entirely from index, no heap access. PostgreSQL: Index Only Scan. Requires: (1) all needed columns in index (key or INCLUDE), (2) visibility map bits set for all pages (all tuples visible). VACUUM updates visibility map. Critical for performance on large read-only tables. GiST (Generalized Search Tree): extensible index architecture. Balanced tree. Each node entry is an indexing key with predicate property. Used for: geometric data types (circle, box, polygon), ranges, network types, full-text. Supported operators: @> (contains), <@ (contained), && (overlaps), etc. GIN (Generalized Inverted Index): For indexing composite data types. Structure: B-tree over extracted keys + posting list/tree per key. Two-phase query: look up keys, then fetch posting lists, combine/intersect, retrieve heap tuples. For JSONB: CREATE INDEX idx_gin ON t USING gin (data jsonb_path_ops); jsonb_path_ops indexes hash of path+value. Efficient for @> (containment). SELECT * FROM t WHERE data @> '{"active":true, "count":5}'; EXPLAIN output: Bitmap Index Scan on idx_gin (rows=50) -> Bitmap Heap Scan on t. Planner estimates: Bitmap Index Scan applies index condition, builds bitmap of TIDs. Bitmap Heap Scan rechecks condition and filters. Sequential scan: Seq Scan on t (rows=1000000) -> slow. Difference: Index Scan (B-tree) directly follows TID chain; fast for few rows. Bitmap Index Scan (B-tree or GIN) gathers TIDs, sorts by block, fetches heap sequentially; good for moderate to many rows. Seq Scan reads whole table. Visual from EXPLAIN ANALYZE: compare actual time and buffers read. Index only scan shows 'Heap Fetches: 0' if VM all-visible.
